term: 变化盲视
oneLiner: 眼前的世界被整个换掉，你也可能毫无察觉。
oneLinerEn: The world in front of you can change drastically and you may never notice.
detail: 经典「换人实验」里，正在问路的实验者被门板一挡、悄悄换成另一个人，超过半数被试毫无察觉。视觉并不像摄像机那样完整记录一切，而是依赖注意逐点「采样」。没被注意到的变化，大脑默认「一切如常」，用错觉把它填补过去。你以为尽收眼底的丰富世界，其实远没有想象中那么牢靠。
detailEn: In the famous door study, a researcher asking for directions was hidden by a passing door and swapped for a different person, and most people never noticed. Vision does not record everything like a camera; it samples point by point, guided by attention. Unattended changes are silently filled in with the assumption that nothing happened. The rich world you feel you see is far less complete than you assume.

term: 盲视
oneLiner: 主观上「什么都看不见」，却能准确避开障碍、猜对光点方向。
oneLinerEn: Reportedly seeing nothing, patients still dodge obstacles and guess light locations accurately.
detail: 初级视觉皮层受损的人，视野里对应的区域自称全盲。可当实验者强迫他们去「猜」目标的位置或运动方向时，正确率却远高于偶然。这说明大脑存在不经过意识视觉通路的第二条「暗线」。我们平常所说的「看见」，只是众多视觉加工里被意识到的那一小层。
detailEn: People with damage to primary visual cortex insist a region of their field is totally blind. Yet when forced to guess a target's location or direction of motion, they perform far above chance. This reveals visual processing routes that bypass conscious sight. What we call seeing is only the thin slice of vision that reaches awareness.

term: 裂脑人与左脑「解释器」
oneLiner: 切断两个半球的联络后，一个头颅里仿佛住着两条各自为政的意识。
oneLinerEn: Sever the two hemispheres and one head seems to house two separate streams of mind.
detail: 为治疗癫痫而切断胼胝体的患者，不会说话的右脑指挥左手做出动作，左脑却立刻编出一个理由，来「解释」这个它毫不知情的行为。神经科学家加扎尼加据此提出「解释器」：大脑里有个不停把碎片拼成连贯故事的模块。你眼中那个统一的「自我」，可能部分是事后编造的叙事。
detailEn: In patients whose corpus callosum was cut to treat epilepsy, the silent right hand can act on a command the speaking left hemisphere never saw, yet it instantly invents a reason for the behaviour. Gazzaniga called this the interpreter: a module that endlessly stitches fragments into a coherent story. The unified self you see may be partly a post-hoc narrative.

term: 记忆的「确信感」可以被制造
termEn: Confidence in Memory Can Be Manufactured
oneLiner: 最生动的回忆未必最准确，那份「我绝对记得」的确信感本身也能被造出来。
oneLinerEn: The most vivid memory is not the most accurate; the sheer certainty of it can be manufactured.
detail: 回忆并不是取回一份存档，而是当场重新拼贴，每拼一次都可能被新问题、新画面悄悄改写。更棘手的是，记忆的主观信心与真实准确度常常脱钩：洛夫斯特只需旁人几句暗示，就能让一部分成年人对一段从未发生过的经历「笃信不疑」，而且越自信答得越果断。也就是说，那份「我清清楚楚记得」的确定感，本身就可以被制造出来。（想彻底破除「记忆像录像带」这一流行说法，见「常见误区」。）
detailEn: Remembering is not retrieving a stored file but reassembling it on the spot, and each reassembly can be quietly edited by a new question or image. Trickier still, the confidence we feel often comes apart from real accuracy: with a few suggestions from a relative, Loftus made some adults firmly believe in an experience that never happened, sure of it the more they answered. The very certainty of 'I remember it clearly' can itself be manufactured. (For a full debunking of the popular 'memory is a video recording' claim, see the Myths section.)

term: 「我决定」出现得比你以为的晚
oneLiner: 在你感到「我要动手」之前，大脑已经提前启动了动作。
oneLinerEn: The brain begins to move before you feel that you have decided to.
detail: Libet 让被试随时机动手指，发现运动前的脑电「准备电位」比他们报告的「决定时刻」早出现数百毫秒。这被解读为：有意识的「决定」或许更像对一个已经启动的过程的追认。但该结论争议极大——准备电位可能只是噪声的累积，而「自由否决权」也仍然留有空间。它真正动摇的，是「意识总是第一推动」这一朴素直觉。
detailEn: Libet asked people to flick a wrist whenever they wished and found that the readiness potential rose hundreds of milliseconds before they reported deciding. This is read as consciousness retroactively endorsing a process already under way. But the claim is hotly disputed: the potential may be mere noise accumulating, and a free won't may still remain. What it really unsettles is the naive sense that awareness is always the first mover.

term: 橡皮手错觉
oneLiner: 同步的抚触，能让大脑把一只假手认领成「我的」。
oneLinerEn: Synchronised touch can make the brain claim a fake hand as its own.
detail: 藏起真手、看着眼前那只橡皮手被同步刷触，几分钟内人们会真切地感到「那是我的手」，甚至在它看似被「威胁」时下意识地缩手、出汗。身体的边界并非天生确定，而是大脑依据多路感觉信号做出的一次「最佳猜测」。连「自我」最基础的拥有感，原来都可以被轻易改写。
detailEn: Hide your real hand and stroke a visible rubber hand in sync, and within minutes people genuinely feel that it is their hand, even flinching or sweating when it seems threatened. The boundary of the body is not a fixed given but the brain's best guess from many sensory signals. Even the most basic sense of owning a body can be quietly rewritten.

term: 选择盲视
oneLiner: 我们常说不清自己为何那样选，还会爱上根本没选的那个。
oneLinerEn: We often cannot say why we chose, and happily embrace the option we never picked.
detail: 被试在两张人脸照片里挑出更有吸引力的那张，实验者却把选中的悄悄换成另一张递回去；多数人不仅没有发现，还兴致勃勃地为「自己从没选过的脸」编起偏好的理由。偏好也许并非从内心流向选择，恰恰相反——我们通过观察自己选了啥，倒推出「原来我喜欢它」的故事。
detailEn: Participants chose the more attractive of two faces; the researcher quietly handed back the one they never picked, and most not only failed to notice but enthusiastically explained why they preferred it. Preference may not flow from mind to choice; instead we infer that we must like it by watching what we chose.

term: 情感预测偏差
oneLiner: 对于「未来会不会开心」，我们的预测差得离谱。
oneLinerEn: We are strikingly bad at predicting how happy we will feel in the future.
detail: 人们普遍高估挂科、失恋、竞选失败带来的长期痛苦，也低估自己走出低谷的速度——大脑有一套被我们严重低估的「情绪免疫系统」。真正左右长期幸福感的，往往并不是我们事先紧绷着迎接的那件事。看明白这一点，能让我们对「想象中的人生转折」少一分执念。
detailEn: People overestimate the lasting pain of a failed exam, a breakup or an election loss, and underestimate how fast they recover, thanks to a psychological immune system they badly under-credit. What actually drives long-term well-being is often not the event we braced ourselves for. Seeing this clearly loosens our grip on the imagined turning point of a life.

term: 享乐适应
oneLiner: 中彩票和意外瘫痪，一年后的幸福感竟差不多。
oneLinerEn: Lottery winners and the recently paralysed report similar happiness a year on.
detail: 布里克曼发现，彩票中奖者的日常快乐并不显著高于普通人，而意外瘫痪者在数月之后情绪已大幅回弹。人被一台「享乐跑步机」拉着往前走，无论好运噩运，都慢慢退回各自的基线。这动摇了「只要得到 X 我就幸福」的直觉——外部境遇的长期影响，远没有我们以为的那么大。
detailEn: Brickman found that lottery winners were no happier day to day than ordinary people, while accident-paralysis victims rebounded emotionally within months. A hedonic treadmill pulls everyone back toward a personal baseline whatever the fortune. This shakes the intuition that once I get X I will be happy; circumstance matters far less over the long run than we think.

term: 语言重塑颜色感知
oneLiner: 母语里有没有「浅蓝 / 深蓝」的分界，会影响你辨别色块的快慢。
oneLinerEn: Whether your language splits light and dark blue changes how fast you tell shades apart.
detail: 俄语把浅蓝和深蓝当作两个基本颜色词。实验显示，俄语者在跨越这条边界的蓝色块辨别上比英语者更快，而当被要求一边默念词语一边判断时，这种优势随即消失。语言未必决定你能不能看见，却能在毫秒之间悄悄拨动知觉最敏感的神经。我们看到的，有一部分是母语替我们提前划好的。
detailEn: Russian treats light blue and dark blue as two basic colour words. Russian speakers are faster at telling shades apart across that boundary, and the edge vanishes when they must hold words in working memory. Language may not decide what you can see, but in milliseconds it nudges perception at its most sensitive point. Part of what we see is drawn for us in advance by our mother tongue.

term: 麦格克效应：眼睛改写耳朵
oneLiner: 看到嘴型是「fa」、听到音是「ba」，你会笃定自己听见了第三个音。
oneLinerEn: See lips say 'fa', hear a 'ba', and you insist you heard a third sound entirely.
detail: 当视频里的口型与真实语音对不上，大脑不会各管各的，而是强行把它们融合成一个你从未被播放过的音节，且当事人毫无察觉。知觉不是被动接收单一感官信号，而是一次多通道「最佳猜测」。你以为纯粹『听到』的东西，其实早被眼睛改写过。
detailEn: When a video's lip movements clash with the real sound, the brain fuses them into a third syllable you were never actually played, and you stay convinced. Perception is not passive reception but a best guess across senses. What you think you purely heard has already been rewritten by what you saw.

term: 音素恢复：丢失的音被『脑补』回来
oneLiner: 句子里一个音被咳嗽声盖掉，你却『清楚听到』那个根本没出现的音。
oneLinerEn: A cough erases one sound, yet you clearly 'hear' the phoneme that was never there.
detail: 沃伦在一句话中抹去一个辅音、换成一声咳嗽，绝大多数听者不仅没察觉缺损，还坚称听到了原本那个音，甚至报告咳嗽其实出现在别处。大脑依据语境默默补全输入，再把它当成感觉本身交给你。知觉的『完整』，有相当一部分是事后填补的假象。
detailEn: Warren replaced a consonant in a sentence with a cough; most listeners not only missed the gap but swore they heard the original sound, some even relocating the cough. The brain silently completes input from context and hands it back as plain sensation. The wholeness of what you perceive is largely post-filled.

term: 双眼竞争：两只眼睛各看到一个世界
oneLiner: 两只眼各看不同图时，知觉不是混合，而是来回『切换』。
oneLinerEn: Give each eye a different image and perception alternates rather than blends.
detail: 左眼放面孔、右眼放房屋，你不会看到两者的叠影，而是一阵只看见面孔、一阵只看见房屋，此消彼长。大脑并不简单地把两路信号平均，而是在两套『假设』间轮流取舍。所谓稳定统一的视觉世界，底下其实是持续不断的争夺。
detailEn: Show a face to one eye and a house to the other and you never see them merged; instead they alternate, one dominating then the other. The brain does not average the two streams but cycles between rival interpretations. Your stable visual world rests on a quiet, ongoing contest.

term: 联觉：能『尝到』声音的感官
oneLiner: 对某些人来说，字母有色、数字在空间里排成地图、声音带着味道。
oneLinerEn: For some, letters have colours, numbers form spatial maps, and sounds carry flavours.
detail: 联觉者的某一种感官会自动、稳定地唤起另一种体验：看到音符就『看见』固定颜色，且多年不变。神经影像显示相关脑区之间存在异常的连接或抑制解除。它说明『五感分立』只是常态而非铁律，感知的边界远比我们以为的可塑。
detailEn: In synaesthesia one sense reliably triggers another: a note is 'seen' as a fixed colour, unchanged for years. Imaging suggests extra links or released inhibition between the relevant areas. It shows our neat five senses are habit, not law, and the boundaries of perception are far more pliable than assumed.

term: 知觉是一种『受控的幻觉』
oneLiner: 大脑是先预测、再用感觉校正，你『看到』的其实是它的最佳猜测。
oneLinerEn: The brain predicts first and corrects with sensation; what you see is its best guess.
detail: 预测加工理论认为，大脑不断向上抛出对外部世界的预测，只把『预测与实际不符』的误差往下传。生动的感觉更接近一次被感官证据约束住的幻觉；做梦、幻觉体验正是这套预测在没有输入时独自运行。我们并非被动看世界，而是在主动『猜』世界。
detailEn: Predictive processing holds that the brain constantly projects forecasts outward and relays only the mismatch back down. Vivid perception is closer to a hallucination kept in check by sensory evidence; dreaming shows the same machinery running with no input at all. We do not passively watch the world but actively guess it.

term: 异族效应：认别人的脸真的更难
oneLiner: 『他们看起来都一样』并非偏见那么简单，而是经验塑造的知觉。
oneLinerEn: 'They all look the same' is less a prejudice than perception shaped by experience.
detail: 人们辨别本族面孔明显优于辨别外族面孔，而这并非天生：三个月的婴儿尚无此偏向，随着接触的构成而变化；给西方婴儿持续输入非洲面孔，其外族效应可被削弱。我们的『看脸』系统是按成长环境精细调校的，见得多才分得清。
detailEn: We tell faces of our own group apart far better than those of another, and this is not innate: three-month-olds show no such bias, and it tracks experience—western infants given steady contact with other-race faces lose the effect. Our face perception is tuned to what we are surround by, expertise by exposure.

term: 鸡尾酒会效应：噪声里锁定自己的名字
oneLiner: 满屋嘈杂，你的耳朵却始终给某个『频道』留着门。
oneLinerEn: Amid the din, one unattended channel stays quietly on watch for you.
detail: 即便你一心专注于和眼前人说话，邻桌忽地提到你的名字，你几乎会立刻察觉；而同样音量、无关的词语却进不了意识。这说明未被注意的输入并没有被完全关在门外，某些有意义的信号（尤其自己的名字）能绕过注意长驱直入。注意的『过滤』远不如想象中决绝。
detailEn: Fully absorbed in one conversation, you still turn at once if a neighbouring table says your name, though equal, less personal words never reach you. Unattended input is not wholly locked out; meaningful signals above all your own name slip past the filter. Attention's gatekeeping is far leakier than it feels.

term: 注意瞬脱：专注后的半秒『失明』
oneLiner: 刚抓住一个重要目标，接下来半秒内你会对第二个目标视而不见。
oneLinerEn: Grab one target and, for half a second, a second one flashes past unseen.
detail: 在一串快速呈现的字母里找出一个数字后，紧随其后的第二个数字常在过去约半秒内『消失』——注意资源被前一个目标占用，留下了一个短暂的盲区。这暴露了意识并非连续录像，而更像间歇采样：一旦注意力被吃满，现实会出现一小段空白。
detailEn: After spotting one target among fast letters, a second that follows within about half a second often vanishes, the prior capture having drained attention. Consciousness, it shows, is not a continuous recording but an intermittent sampling; feed it a demand and reality briefly blanks.

term: 『多任务』其实是快速切换
oneLiner: 所谓一心多用，大脑只是在任务间来回切换并为此付费。
oneLinerEn: 'Multitasking' is the brain flip-flopping between jobs and paying a toll.
detail: 每当从一个任务切到另一个，反应都会变慢、更易出错，这段『切换代价』在频繁来回时不断累加。并行处理只发生在少数自动化的技能上；对需要注意的事情，人脑其实一次只够做一件。『边……边……』的流畅感，掩盖了每一次重新对焦的隐性开销。
detailEn: Each time we switch from one task to another we slow down and err more, and this switch cost piles up with every flip. Genuine parallel work is left to a few automatized skills; for anything demanding attention the brain does one thing at a time. The ease of 'doing it all' hides the cost of each refocus.

term: 半侧忽略：被『删掉』的一半世界
oneLiner: 有的病人并非看不见左半边，而是根本『不觉得它存在』。
oneLinerEn: Some patients do not fail to see the left world; it fails to register at all.
detail: 右顶叶受损的人可能只吃盘子的右半边、只画一半的房子，却对缺失毫无自觉，甚至否认左侧身体属于自己。关键在于这不是感觉输入坏了，而是注意与意识表征塌了一半。它逼我们追问：『看见』需要多少注意的参与？
detailEn: After right-parietal damage people eat only the right of a plate, draw half a house, and lack any insight the rest exists. The sense-data are fine; it is attention and conscious representation that have collapsed on one side, forcing the question of how much attention seeing really needs.

term: 孤立效应：唯一不同的那个最难忘
oneLiner: 一整片相同里那个突兀的『异类』，你会记得最牢。
oneLinerEn: The lone oddity amid a uniform field is the one you remember best.
detail: 在一串同类项目里，唯一与众不同的那一项更容易被记住（一个数字混进一堆单词，或一个红词夹在一堆黑词里）。大脑靠『对比』而非『次数』来挑出值得保存的信息，独特性本身就是记忆优势。这解释了为何特立独行的品牌、事件在记忆里格外显眼。
detailEn: In a list of like items the one distinctive element is best remembered—a digit among words, one red word among black. Memory selects by contrast rather than repetition, so distinctness itself confers an edge, which is why the outlier brand or event looms large.

term: 峰终定律：体验只被『高点』和『结尾』记分
oneLiner: 评价一段经历，大脑几乎只取最痛的一刻和最后一刻。
oneLinerEn: Judge an experience and the brain samples only its peak and its last moment.
detail: 肠镜实验里，被拉长但结尾更温和的那次，事后被记住的不适反而更低、更愿意复查，尽管全程累积的疼痛明显更多。我们对一段体验的『记忆评分』不等于体验本身：时长常被忽略，峰值与结尾却主宰回忆。这会悄悄反过来塑造我们日后的选择。
detailEn: A colonoscopy made longer yet gentler at the end was remembered as less bad and more willingly repeated, despite more total pain. Our remembered rating of an experience diverges from the experience itself: duration is neglected while peak and ending rule, quietly steering the choices that follow.

term: 闪光灯记忆：生动不等于准确
oneLiner: 对重大时刻『历历在目』的自信，与实际准确度并不同步。
oneLinerEn: Vivid 'I saw it all' certainty about historic events tracks confidence, not accuracy.
detail: 塔拉里科和鲁宾在 9/11 次日及随后数月反复询问人们当时在哪、如何得知。人们对自己记忆的信心一路高涨，细节却照样在几周里悄悄出错、走样。强烈情绪让记忆『感觉』格外真实，却并不给它加固；这份确信感本身就值得警惕（对照『记忆的『确信感』可以被制造』）。
detailEn: Talarico and Rubin re-questioned people the day after 9/11 and again over months: confidence in their memories climbed while the details aged and erred just like ordinary ones. Strong emotion makes a memory feel true without actually preserving it; the certainty itself deserves suspicion.

term: 记忆被文化图式『同化』
oneLiner: 复述一个陌生故事，你会不知不觉把它改得符合自己的文化套路。
oneLinerEn: Retell an unfamiliar tale and it drifts, unbidden, into the shapes your culture expects.
detail: 巴特莱特让人反复复述一幅原住民的『鬼的战争』图画。每一次转述都更短、更合逻辑，那些与本土常识格格不入的超自然细节被逐步抹平或改写成说得通的版本。记忆不是存档而是按『图式』重构；我们记住的，常常是被自身文化加工过的版本。
detailEn: Bartlett had people repeatedly retell a native 'War of the Ghosts' story. Each telling grew shorter and tidier, its alien supernatural details smoothed into sensible versions. Memory is not a stored record but a reconstruction by schemas; what we keep is often the culturally edited edition.

term: 情绪消退偏差：坏情绪比好情绪散得快
oneLiner: 回忆往事时，负面事件附带的情绪淡得比正面的更快。
oneLinerEn: Recalling the past, the feelings tied to bad events fade faster than the good.
detail: 沃克等人发现，人们报告旧事时，消极事件唤起的情绪随时间消退得比积极事件更明显——同一件难过的往事，如今回想已波澜不惊，而一件开心往事仍余味盎然。这套『给记忆调色』的机制可能有助于自我整合与心理健康，它悄悄改写着我们对过去的感受。
detailEn: Walker and colleagues found that the emotion attached to negative memories fades more steeply over time than that attached to positive ones—the same sad event now barely stirs while a glad one still glows. This 'memory shading' may aid well-being, quietly rewriting how the past feels.

term: 心盲症：脑中放不出一幅画面
oneLiner: 有人闭上眼能历历在目，有人却只能『知道』却『看不见』。
oneLinerEn: Some close their eyes and see vividly; others can only 'know', never 'see'.
detail: 泽曼描述了一批自愿想象不出任何画面的人：请他们想一只苹果，他们清楚知道苹果的概念，眼前却一片漆黑。过去几乎无人意识到『脑内成像』存在个体有无之差。它揭开了意识的一个盲区：同一句『想象一下』，在不同头脑里唤起的是全然不同的体验。
detailEn: Zeman described people who cannot summon any mental image: asked to picture an apple they know the word well yet see nothing. Until then few realised inner imagery varied from person to person. It exposes a blind spot in consciousness: the same 'just imagine' kindles utterly different worlds in different minds.

term: 脸盲症：认不出任何面孔
oneLiner: 有人看亲人和看路人一样陌生，只能靠发型与声音认人。
oneLinerEn: For some, a loved one's face is as unreadable as a stranger's—known only by hair and voice.
detail: 脸盲者视力正常、能描摹五官细节，却无法把一张脸识别为『谁』，甚至认不出镜中的自己。面孔并非由『一般物体识别』处理，而有专门、易损的神经 machinery。你以为天经地义的『看脸识人』，原来是脑中一座可能单独断电的专楼。
detailEn: Prosopagnosics see normally, can trace features, yet cannot tell a face—who it belongs to—even in the mirror. Faces are handled not by generic object vision but by dedicated, fragile machinery. Effortless 'seeing a face as someone' turns out to be one special storey of the brain that can go dark alone.

term: 幻肢痛与镜盒疗法
termEn: Phantom Limb and the Mirror Box
oneLiner: 截去的手臂仍能『痛』，一面镜子却能让它停止抽痛。
oneLinerEn: An amputated arm can still ache—yet a plain mirror can quiet the pain.
detail: 失去肢体的人常感到那只手仍在、甚至剧痛挛缩。拉马钱德兰让患者望向镜盒，用仅存的手映出『失去的手』正常活动，许多人竟感到幻肢松开了、疼痛减轻。痛信号来自大脑对身体图的预期，而非肢体本身。连『身体边界』都只是一份可被视觉说服的模型。
detailEn: The lost limb is often still felt, sometimes clenched in pain. Ramachandran had patients watch a mirror box that showed the missing hand moving normally via the surviving one; many felt it unclench and ease. The pain signal comes from the brain's predicted body map, not the limb. Even the body's edge is a model persuasion can rewrite.

term: 卡普格拉综合征：亲人被『掉包』了
oneLiner: 认得出母亲的脸，却坚称她是完美的冒充者。
oneLinerEn: The face is recognised as your mother's, yet you insist an impostor stands in her place.
detail: 某些患者能准确认出亲人，却说『他看起来像，但绝不是他』。解释指向一条断裂的通路：面孔识别完好，却接不上那份自动的『熟悉感／情感反应』。于是大脑为矛盾找了一个自洽的说法——这是替身。它让人看到：『亲切感』原来是一条可断的独立回路。
detailEn: Some patients correctly identify a relative yet insist, 'He looks like him but is not him.' The account: a severed route—face recognition intact but uncoupled from the warm feeling of familiarity. The brain resolves the clash with a coherent story: an impostor. Warmth, it reveals, is its own breakable circuit.

term: 科塔尔德综合征：确信自己已经死了
oneLiner: 极少数人在意识清醒时，真诚地相信自己已不复存在。
oneLinerEn: A rare few, fully lucid, come to believe in earnest that they no longer exist.
detail: 科塔尔德综合征患者声称自己已死、器官在腐烂、或根本不存在，甚至拒绝进食因为『死人不需吃』。它常与严重抑郁、躯体感觉通路异常有关。当构成『我还活着』那种基底情感体验的信号被抹去，连存在感本身都可能坍塌——自我并非不碎的铁板。
detailEn: Cotard patients claim they are dead, decaying, or do not exist, sometimes refusing food because 'the dead need not eat'. Linked to severe depression and disrupted bodily-awareness pathways, it shows that when the background feeling of being alive is erased even existence can collapse: self is no seamless given.

term: 镜像测试：谁认得出镜子里是自己
oneLiner: 黑猩猩能认出镜子中的自己，大多灵长类却不能。
oneLinerEn: Apes recognise themselves in a mirror; many other primates do not.
detail: 盖洛普用『镜子＋麻醉后额上一点红』测试：只有当动物照镜时去摸自己额上的红点，才说明它知道『镜里那个＝我』。黑猩猩、猩猩、海豚、大喙鸦能过，狝狲、大多灵长类则对镜攻击或忽视。『自我认知』可能并非人类独有，也并非高等动物的标配，而是特定社交生态下的演化产物。
detailEn: Gallup's mirror-plus-red-spot test counts as passing only if the anaesthetised animal, seeing the mirror, touches its own mark. Apes, dolphins and magpies pass; monkeys mostly attack or ignore it. Self-recognition may be neither uniquely human nor a given for smart animals but a product of particular social niches.

term: 名字字母效应：暗地里偏爱自己的字母
oneLiner: 你对自己姓名里的字母和数字，有一种说不出口的偏爱。
oneLinerEn: You hold an unspoken fondness for the very letters inside your own name.
detail: 纳坦发现，人们评价 26 个字母时系统性地高估自己姓名中出现的那些，且自己并不承认这份偏向。偏好会在无意识里围绕『自我』打转（内隐自尊）。连选品牌、选城市、选配偶姓这样的大事，都可能被名字里几个毫不起眼的字母悄悄拨动。
detailEn: Nuttin found people rate the letters in their own name higher than others, without owning the bias. Preference orbits the self below awareness (implicit self-esteem); even brands, cities and surnames can be nudged by a few unremarkable letters.

term: 内省错觉：我们其实看不透自己
oneLiner: 对于『我为何这么做』，我们的内省并不比旁人更可靠。
oneLinerEn: On 'why I did that', our own introspection is no more reliable than an outsider's.
detail: 尼斯贝特与威尔逊显示，人们能准确报告结果（选了啥、有啥感受），却对『过程』——是什么真正影响了他们——往往误判，然后凭常识编出一个看似合理的理由。我们对自己的心理，更像拿着结论的外人而非掌权的上帝。这与『选择盲视』『裂脑解释器』同属一条震撼的线索。
detailEn: Nisbett and Wilson showed people report outcomes accurately yet misjudge the process—what truly swayed them—then invent commonsense reasons. We are less the owner of our minds than a bystander holding the verdict. It joins choice blindness and the split-brain interpreter as one disquieting thread.

term: 观念运动效应：思想自己动了手
oneLiner: 占卜盘、笔仙的移动，往往来自你毫无察觉的微小手劲。
oneLinerEn: Ouija's move usually comes from tiny forces you never feel yourself applying.
detail: 卡本特提出：一旦在脑中强烈地想着一个动作，身体就会几乎不走意识地把它执行出来。这就是降神桌上指针自己跑的根源——不是鬼神，而是参与者不自觉的微动叠加。『是我在做还是它自己在动』的边界，比我们以为的模糊得多。
detailEn: Carpenter held that vividly thinking an act sets the body almost quietly performing it—the real engine of the moving planchette, not spirits but participants' unnoticed pressures. The border between 'I am moving it' and 'it moves itself' is far blurier than we admit.

term: 假手术也能『治好』
oneLiner: 只做切口不真正动手的假手术，止痛效果常与真手术相当。
oneLinerEn: A cut with no real operation often relieves as much as the genuine article.
detail: 莫斯利等给膝关节炎患者做关节镜，三分一组：真清理、只做切口、仅打麻醉。一年后三组改善大致相当。当『被治疗』的预期、仪式与关怀足够强烈，身体会自己交出一份康复。安慰剂不是『编出来的病』，而是真实生理通路被信念点燃了。
detailEn: Moseley gave knee-arthritis patients arthroscopy in three arms: real clean-up, incision only, anaesthesia alone. A year on, all improved about equally. When expectation, ritual and care are strong enough, the body delivers its own recovery. Placebo is no illusion; belief ignites real physiology.

term: 反安慰剂：坏预期真能伤你
oneLiner: 被告知会痛，人就真的更痛；被预告副作用，副作用就多。
oneLinerEn: Warn of pain and it hurts more; forecast side effects and people report more.
detail: 与安慰剂相反，纯粹出于负面预期的症状恶化叫反安慰剂：被预告恶心的病人更容易吐，被告知会痛的测试中确实报告了更多痛。预期不仅修饰感受，还能制造真实的不适。它提醒医学：一句『这个可能会有点痛』，本身就成了治疗的一部分。
detailEn: The mirror of placebo, nocebo is worsening driven purely by negative expectation: patients warned of nausea retch more, those told it will hurt report more pain. Expectation not only colours sensation but manufactures it—a clinical reminder that 'this may sting' is itself part of the treatment.

term: 吊桥效应：心跳会找错对象
oneLiner: 摇晃吊桥上遇到的陌生人，更容易被当成『心动』。
oneLinerEn: A stranger met on a shaky suspension bridge is likelier read as a flutter of the heart.
detail: 达顿与阿伦让男子走过晃悠的悬索桥或安稳的石桥，事后给一位女实验者的电话。刚走过险桥的人更易拨打、也更易把她描述成有吸引力。生理唤醒（心跳、手抖）是中性的，大脑会给它套上一个『此刻眼前』的理由。所谓一见钟情，部分只是心跳认错了归因。
detailEn: Dutton and Aron had men cross a wobbly suspension bridge or a steady one, then phone an attractive researcher. Those fresh off the scary bridge called more and rated her more appealing. Arousal is neutral; the brain dresses it in whatever reason is at hand. Love at first sight is partly a misfiled racing pulse.

term: 情绪是大脑建构出来的
oneLiner: 『愤怒』『恐俱』并非脸上天生写好的节目，而是被概念现场拼成。
oneLinerEn: 'Anger' and 'fear' are not hard-wired programs but assembled on the spot by concepts.
detail: 建构论认为，同样的心跳加速、同样紧锁的眉头，在不同情境与不同概念下会被塑造为不同的『情绪』；身体反应本身并不自带一张固定的情绪标签。情绪与其说是发现，不如说是大脑用过往经验即时制造的解释。它把『人人共有同一种表情』的朴素直觉松动了不少。
detailEn: On the constructed view, the same racing heart and furrowed brow become different emotions under different context and concepts; bodily changes carry no fixed label of their own. Emotion is less found than made—an explanation the brain builds in real time from past experience, loosening the naive idea of universal built-in expressions.

term: 负面偏差：坏比好更有『分量』
oneLiner: 一句批评的杀伤力，往往大于一堆赞美。
oneLinerEn: One criticism usually outweighs a heap of praise.
detail: 伊藤等用生理测量发现，负面刺激比同等强度的正面刺激唤起更强的反应。从记忆、判断到情绪，『坏』享有系统性的优势——因为快速侦测威胁在演化上更致命。理解了这条不对称，就能明白为何幸福难以堆叠、却容易被一件坏事击穿。
detailEn: Ito and colleagues found negative stimuli recruit larger physiological responses than equally strong positive ones. Badness holds a systematic edge across memory, judgment and affect—fast threat detection was the costlier bet. Knowing this asymmetry explains why well-being stacks slowly yet is punctured easily by one bad thing.

term: 躯体标记：身体比头脑先『知道』
oneLiner: 还没想明白，手心已出汗：身体先把『该避开』的信号送了上来。
oneLinerEn: Before you reason it out, your palms sweat: the body flags 'avoid this' first.
detail: 达马西奥的赌博任务里，健康人在反复摸到『坑人的牌堆』后，尚未意识到规则时手心就已先出汗，身体先于意识发出警告。而腹内侧前额叶受损者没有这种信号，明知吃亏仍不断下注。理性未必高踞于身体之上，直觉常是躯体经验悄悄递交的证据。
detailEn: In Damasio's gambling task, healthy players sweat over the losing deck before they can explain the rule—the body flags danger ahead of awareness. Patients with ventromedial damage, lacking that signal, keep choosing it to their cost. Reason may not sit atop the body; gut feeling is bodily experience handed up as evidence.

term: 选择悖论：选项越多越不快乐
oneLiner: 面对二十四果酱，人们反而不如面对六种时买得多、也选得开心。
oneLinerEn: Twenty-four jams sell less and satisfy less than six.
detail: 亚格纳与莱珀在超市摆摊：一大排试吃选择吸引了更多人驻足，却更少人真的购买；选择有限那一组反倒更满意自己的决定。选项爆炸会抬高期待、加重权衡成本、并让人事后更容易后悔。『越多越自由』的直觉，在心理账户上未必成立。
detailEn: Iyengar and Lepper set up a tasting booth: an enormous array drew more browsers yet far fewer buyers, while the smaller set left people likelier to feel they'd chosen well. A glut of options raises expectations, magnifies trade-offs and invites regret. More choice as more freedom does not always hold.

term: 冷热共情鸿沟：冷静时猜不透激情的自己
oneLiner: 饱腹时低估饥饿，冷静时低估冲动——我们总用『现在的自己』去预测『别的自己』。
oneLinerEn: Fed, we underrate hunger; calm, we underrate passion—predicting other selves from who we are now.
detail: 亚里埃利等发现，处于某种驱动状态（饿、冷、性唤起、愤怒）时，人极难准确预测自己在相反状态下的感受与决定；反之也一样。我们习惯把当下状态当成『通用状态』，把还没上任的那个自己估得太轻。这解释了为何计划总在情绪来袭时纷纷失效。
detailEn: Ariely and colleagues found that in a driven state—hunger, cold, arousal, anger—we badly misjudge how we'll feel and choose in its absence, and the reverse holds too. We treat our present mood as the neutral default and underweight the not-yet-arrived self. It is why plans buckle when feeling shows up.

term: 规划谬误：计划总比想象慢
oneLiner: 无论多少经验，我们几乎总是低估一件事要多久。
oneLinerEn: However often we've been wrong, we still under-predict how long things take.
detail: 比勒等人让被试预估论文、作业、个人目标的完工日，绝大多数系统性地乐观、一再延期，且上一次超时并不能纠正下一次的估计。我们会构想一个『一切顺利』的理想剧本，却给『意外』几乎不留预算。破解办法常是参照同类事情的『外部实际耗时』。
detailEn: Buehler and colleagues had people date their theses, tasks and goals; estimates ran consistently optimistic and were repeatedly blown, with past overruns failing to cure the next one. We script a best-case plan and budget almost nothing for mishaps. The fix is often to anchor on how long such things actually took before.

term: 赌徒谬误：相信随机会『找平』
oneLiner: 轮盘连开七次红，很多人却坚信下一次『该』是黑。
oneLinerEn: After seven reds, many are sure the next spin 'must' come up black.
detail: 特沃斯基与卡尼曼指出，人们期待小样本也像大样本那样『代表』总体，于是以为随机会自我补偿。硬币没有记忆，独立事件不会因为你等了久就改变概率。这种『欠公平』直觉与『热手』恰好相反，却同源于我们拿『看起来该长啥样』替代了『真实概率是多少』。
detailEn: Tversky and Kahneman showed people expect small samples to represent the population, so they think chance will self-correct. Coins have no memory; independent events do not turn your way because you've waited. This 'owed fairness' intuition is the mirror image of the hot hand, both stemming from substituting looks-right for real probability.

term: 热手错觉：连中并不预示着下一投
oneLiner: 篮球员连投几个，观众更赌下一个也进，数据却说这只是噪声。
oneLinerEn: After a streak, crowds bet the next shot drops too; the data say it is just noise.
detail: 吉洛维奇等分析 NBA 罚球与投篮数据，发现上一投命中并不会真正抬高下一投命中的概率，与球迷和球员的『他今天手正热』直觉相反。我们在随机序列里执意读出连串与势头，这恰与『赌徒谬误』构成一正一反的双面错觉：世界多半没那么懂『因果』，是我们非要给它安排剧情。
detailEn: Gilovich and colleagues found a made shot did not raise the odds of the next, against the vivid 'he's hot' sense of fans and players. We insist on reading streaks and momentum into randomness. The mirror of the gambler's fallacy, both reveal a world less narrative than our craving for plot.

term: 皮格马利翁效应：期待塑造表现
oneLiner: 被随机贴上『潜力股』标签的孩子，学年末真就测得更优。
oneLinerEn: Children labelled 'bloomers' at random genuinely rose by year's end.
detail: 罗森塔尔与雅各布森在一所小学随机挑出一批学生，谎称他们智商测验显示即将爆发潜力。一学年后，这批『被期待』的孩子成绩与智商真就高于对照组。老师的期待可能通过眼神、提问、反馈悄悄改变了相处。他人的信念能反过来塑造一个人——这既令人警醒，也意味着期待本身就是资源。
detailEn: Rosenthal and Jacobson, at random, told a school a handful of pupils were about to bloom; a year on those 'bloomers' outscored peers on IQ and grades. Expectation seemed to leak through glances, questions and feedback. Others' beliefs can make us—both a warning and a lever, for belief is itself a resource.

term: 聚光灯效应：没人在意你的糗
oneLiner: 你为身上那块尴尬的污点焦虑不已，别人却几乎根本没注意到。
oneLinerEn: You agonise over the stain on your shirt; almost no one else clocked it.
detail: 吉洛维奇让被试穿上一件尴尬的T恤走进拥挤房间，他预估半数人会记得这件衣服，实际只有约一半的一半。我们活在自己体验的绝对中心，于是把这份『显眼感』投射给别人，大大高估了外界对自己失误的关注。放下这份聚光灯，往往能活得更轻松。
detailEn: Gilovich had people wear a laughable shirt into a crowded room; they guessed half noticed, when only a quarter did. We live centred in our own experience and project that salience onto others, overestimating by far how much our slipouts are watched. Stepping out of the spotlight is liberating.

term: 虚假共识：以为大家都和我一样
oneLiner: 我们高估了自己的观点、习惯的普遍性，把『我的』当成了『大家的』。
oneLinerEn: We overestimate how shared our own views and habits are, mistaking 'mine' for 'everyone's'.
detail: 罗斯等人发现，无论自己选什么、抱什么态度，人们都系统性地以为多数人会与自己一致，且对反方评价更苛刻。我们的私人经验太顺理成章，以至于忘了它是从无数偶然里长出的一份样本。『这不是很明显吗？』里的『明显』，往往只是『对我而言』。
detailEn: Ross and colleagues found that whatever we choose or believe, we assume most would agree and judge dissenters more harshly. Our private experience feels so obvious we forget it is one sample among countless. The 'obvious' in 'isn't it obvious?' usually means only 'to me'.

term: 公平世界信念：把遭遇重新包装成『应得』
oneLiner: 目睹了不幸，大脑爱反推他『多半咎由自取』，好让世界显得安全。
oneLinerEn: Witness misfortune and the mind retcons the victim as deserving it, to keep the world feeling safe.
detail: 勒纳提出，人们深层需要相信世界公平、善有善报；当这个信念撞上无妄之灾，大脑就倾向于归因于受害者自身（责怪受害人），以维护一种可控感。它安抚了『这事不会发生在我身上』的安心，却以冷酷为代价。道德直觉有时只是焦虑的合理化。
detailEn: Lerner held that we need to believe the world is fair; when that meets unprovoked disaster, the mind blames the victim to keep control. It soothes 'that won't happen to me' at a cruel price—moral judgment can be anxiety wearing reason's mask.

term: 刻板印象威胁：怕印证偏见反而拖累你
oneLiner: 答题前先提醒『女生空间差』，女生就真考得不如平时。
oneLinerEn: Prime 'women are worse at space' before a test and women perform worse than usual.
detail: 斯蒂尔与阿伦森让同等水平的黑人与白人学生参加言语测验：当测试被说成『衡量智力』，差距浮现；当被说成『练习』，差距几乎消失。当人怕把自己群体的负面刻板印象坐实，这份焦虑会占用认知资源、拖累发挥。（注：后续重复研究结果不一，效应存在争议，宜谨慎看待。）
detailEn: When equally able students took a verbal test framed as 'measuring ability', a gap appeared; framed as practice, it mostly vanished. The worry of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group steals working memory and depresses performance. (Later replications are mixed, so treat the effect with caution.)

term: 知识的诅咒：知道了就难以想象不知道
oneLiner: 一旦你懂了一件事，就很难再站回『不懂』的那一边。
oneLinerEn: Once you know a thing, you can barely imagine not knowing it.
detail: 懂敲节拍的实验者自信地以为听众能听出歌曲，听众猜中率却低得可怜——因为旋律在实验者脑中太响亮，他删不掉那个『内部音轨』。我们一旦掌握信息，就很难估计别人在信息缺失时的样子。好的表达、教学与同理，都要刻意地『倒回无知』。
detailEn: Tappers sure their tapped rhythm was obvious were heard as gibberish: the melody is too loud in the tapper's head to switch off. Once we hold information we can't estimate the mind that lacks it. Clear speech, teaching and empathy all take deliberate work to rewind toward ignorance.

term: 麦克白效应：洗手能『洗掉』内疚
oneLiner: 做了亏事后，人会更强地想清洗自己，而洗完真的舒坦些。
oneLinerEn: After a misdeed we crave to wash; scrubbing genuinely eases the stain.
detail: 钟与利连奎斯特发现，回想一件不道德往事后，人们更倾向选择清洁用品；而真洗手后，对那件事的『道德负罪感』会减弱。身体层面的『洁净—不洁』隐喻被借来调节心理层面的罪。它暗示道德感并不纯粹抽象，而与身体感受深绑在一起（此类具身效应的稳健性仍在争论中）。
detailEn: Zhong and Liljenquist found that recalling an unethical act raises the urge to clean, and actually washing lessens felt guilt. The physical clean-dirty metaphor is borrowed to manage moral stain—suggesting conscience is bound to bodily feeling. (The robustness of such embodied effects is still debated.)

term: 道德直觉主义：先判对错，再找理由
oneLiner: 我们对错事的愤怒来得飞快，推理只是事后追补。
oneLinerEn: Our outrage at a wrong arrives fast; the reasoning is a later rider.
detail: 海特提出，道德判断大多是瞬间直觉（『就是不对！』）先行，理性多是为这一直觉找台阶下的『新闻发言人』。他设计的那些『无害却让人不适』的情景（如对空无人的禁忌行为），多数人说不清危害却仍觉得错，正是直觉先于论证的证据。我们的道德推理常常是律师而非法官。
detailEn: Haidt argued that moral judgment is largely instantaneous intuition ('that's just wrong!') with reason as its press secretary. His harmless-yet-offensive scenarios show people insisting on wrongness they cannot justify: the signature of intuition front-running argument. Our moral reason is often a lawyer, not a judge.

term: 道德许可：做了好事之后更容易放纵
oneLiner: 刚刷了『好人卡』，下一步反而更容易破戒或偏心。
oneLinerEn: Bank a good deed and the next step grows easier to slack or show favour.
detail: 乔丹等人发现，哪怕只是在心里回想一件自己做过的善举，或声明自己并不偏见，接下来人们就更允许自己任性——买更贵的东西、选男性候选人、拖延正事。自我形象一旦『被存了钱』，就像获得了消费额。道德动机因此充满陷阱：越自我肯定，可能越容易走偏。
detailEn: Jordan and colleagues found that merely recalling one's own good deed, or declaring oneself unbiased, licenses the next indulgence—pricier buys, picking a male candidate, skipping a duty. Once the moral account is 'funded', it feels spendable. A trap for virtue: the more self-assured, the easier to stray.

term: 外语效应：换种语言，人更理性
oneLiner: 用母语时会情绪化、偏眼前；换成外语，反而更冷静、更讲逻辑。
oneLinerEn: In your mother tongue we feel and jump; in a foreign one, we cool and calculate.
detail: 凯萨等人发现，用非母语思考、决断时，人们更少陷入『框架效应』、更少凭直觉偏向、也更愿为长远取舍。外语在心理上的『疏离感』削低了情绪的牵引，把决策推向更冷的系统。我们以为语言只是表达工具，却不知它也在悄然改写我们思考与取舍的方式。
detailEn: Keysar and colleagues found that thinking and deciding in a non-native tongue dampens framing effects, curbs intuitive biases and favours long-run trade-offs. Foreign-language distance cools emotional pull and nudges choices toward the colder system. Language seems a neutral medium but quietly reshapes how we reason and weigh.

term: 能力观改变坚持：你信不信人能变
oneLiner: 相信能力可长的人，面对挫败更扛得住、也真能进得更多。
oneLinerEn: Those who believe ability grows endure setbacks better and gain more.
detail: 布莱克韦尔与德韦克追踪发现，把智能看作『可拓展』的学生，遇到难题更像去攻尖；把它看作固定天赋的学生，一遇挫就易放弃。同一件事失败，一个读作『我还不行（还没）』，一个读作『我不行』。不过需诚实指出：后续大规模重复中效应比原研究小且不稳，宜理性看待。（对照『智商天生固定』的迷思）
detailEn: Blackwell and Dweck tracked students who saw intelligence as expandable approaching hard tasks versus those seeing it fixed giving in sooner; the same failure read as 'not yet' versus 'not able'. Be honest: large later replications find smaller, shakier effects, so weigh it calmly.

term: 过度辩护：奖励会挤走内在兴趣
oneLiner: 本爱画画的孩子，开始为奖品画后，没了奖品就不画了。
oneLinerEn: Reward a child who loves drawing, and without the reward they stop.
detail: 莱珀等人让爱画画的幼儿承诺得到奖品后才画，几周后他们的自发作画兴趣反低于未受奖组。外在报酬会把『我为自己而做』改写成『我为报酬而做』，一旦报酬消失，动力也搭上了。动机不是越激励越强，有时反而是被激励出来的兴趣谋杀了原有的兴趣。
detailEn: Lepper and colleagues had preschoolers who loved drawing promise a reward to draw; weeks later their free-play interest sank below the unrewarded group. External pay recodes 'I do this for me' into 'I do this for the prize', and when the prize goes so does the drive. Incentives can kill the very interest they borrowed.

term: 习得性无助：无法逃脱后，能逃也不逃了
oneLiner: 反复经历『怎么都没用』，就算门开着，也不再推。
oneLinerEn: Fail enough to escape and you stop trying even when the door stands open.
detail: 塞利格曼先让狗经历无论做什么都无法避开电击的阶段，再把它们放进能轻松跳过的装置，多数却趴着不动、呜咽接受。它们学到的是『一切皆不可控』而非『做不到』。这一模型被类比到抑郁与长期困境：当可控感被反复抹去，人也会放弃本可拥有的选择。
detailEn: Seligman first exposed dogs to shocks no action could stop, then placed them where escape was trivial; many lay down and whined instead of jumping. What they learned was 'nothing I do matters', not 'I can't'. The model maps onto depression: when control is erased often enough, people abandon options still within reach.

term: 必要难度：更难反而记得更牢
oneLiner: 当下越显吃力、越不顺畅的学法，长期往往记得更牢。
oneLinerEn: What feels harder and less smooth now often sticks longer later.
detail: 比约克发现，那些让练习看起来更糟的安排——拉开间隔、打乱题型、先自测再读——当下表现差，延后却记得更好。因为费劲的提取把记忆编得更深。流畅感并不可靠：读得越顺、越觉得自己掌了，实际可能越浅。这直接挑战了『学得很爽=学得好』的直觉。
detailEn: Bjork found that arrangements which make practice look worse—spaced, interleaved, self-tested first—hurt now but help later, effortful retrieval encoding memory more deeply. Fluency misleads: the smoother it reads, the shallower it may sit. It strikes hard at the sense that easy equals learned.

term: 提取练习：考试本身就是最好的学习
oneLiner: 与其反复重读，不如合上书试着回忆——考一次胜读三遍。
oneLinerEn: Rather than reread, close the book and recall—once quizzed beats thrice reviewed.
detail: 勒迪格与卡尔皮克让两组背同一段文字：一组反复重读，一组做一次回忆测试。一周后再考，当初只『考过一次』的那组记得明显更多，尽管他们当时觉得自己掌得不牢。提取不只在检验记忆，它本身就重塑、强化了记忆。最容易被高估的，正是‘试一下’的力量。
detailEn: Roediger and Karpicke had groups study a passage by rereading or by a single recall test; a week later the once-tested group recalled far more despite feeling less sure. Retrieval is not merely checking memory but reshaping it. The underestimated power is simply trying to recall.

term: 婴儿比皮亚杰以为的更『懂物理』
termEn: Infants Know More Than Piaget Thought
oneLiner: 几个月大的婴儿就期待物体延续，只丌是『不会找』而‘没想到去找’。
oneLinerEn: Young infants already expect objects to persist; they just can't yet act on it.
detail: 贝亚日隆用『违反期待』的看时长法让几月大的婴儿看魔术般的障藏：当物体本该在却被移走，婴儿盯着反常一幕明显更久。这说明物体恒存的概念远比武台动作要早上出现。皮亚杰那句『小婴儿没有客体恒常性』，很可能低估了那些『懂但做不到』的孩子。
detailEn: Baillargeon's looking-time method showed months-old infants staring longer when a hidden object vanished impossibly: object permanence is present far before the manual skill to seek it. Piaget's 'infants lack object permanence' likely underrated minds that knew but could not yet act.

term: 婴儿靠统计‘切’出词语
oneLiner: 宝宝没人在教语法，却已靠音节概率把连成一片的声音切成词。
oneLinerEn: With no one teaching grammar, infants slice the sound-stream by syllable odds.
detail: 萨弗兰等让八个月大的婴儿听一段无停顿、人工语言的‘滔滔不绝’，仅两分钟后他们就能听出哪些音节常相邻、哪些不该搭配，从而‘听’出词的边界。原来婴儿的大脑是个不知疲倦的统计机器，在没人手把手教词前，就先从概率里捕捉到了结构。
detailEn: Saffran and colleagues had eight-month-olds hear an unbroken artificial ‘language’; after two minutes they picked out which syllables co-occurred and thus where words began. The infant brain is a tireless statistician, finding structure in the stream before anyone labels a word.

term: 猴子也知道‘自己不知道’
termEn: Animals Know That They Don't Know
oneLiner: 面对难题，狝狲宁可放弃得分去选‘我不知道’，也不乱猜。
oneLinerEn: Faced with a hard test, a monkey forgoes points to say 'I don't know' rather than guess.
detail: 史密斯等人发现，当题目太难，狝狲会选一个‘退出’选项而不坚持作答，以免乱猜受罚——这意味着它能评估自己的掌握度。元认知（对认知的认知）曾被视为人类专属；若动物也懂‘我知不道’，那么‘意识到自己无知’这种高阶能力，可能比想象中古老。
detailEn: Smith and colleagues found that when a test was too hard a monkey chose to opt out rather than risk a wrong guess—implying it read its own confidence. Metacognition was once deemed uniquely human; if animals know they don't know, this insight may be older than we assumed.

term: 松鸦记得‘何时藏了什么’
oneLiner: 藏食的鸟会记得哪块已坏、不该再去挖，仿佛有‘情景记忆’。
oneLinerEn: A caching bird recalls which hoard has rotted and skips it, as if reliving the scene.
detail: 克莱顿与狄金森发现，松鸦藏下易坏与耐存两类食物，经过足够时间后它会先去挖耐存的、跳过已变质的易坏食物，哪怕当下并不饿。这被解读为‘情景样记忆’：记得那次‘何时在哪藏了什么’。情景记忆曾被当作人类专属，如今在一只鸟身上看到了雏形。
detailEn: Clayton and Dickinson found scrub jays that cache perishable and sturdy food return, after a delay, to the sturdy and skip the rotted perishable even when not hungry. Read as episodic-like memory—remembering what-was-where-when. Once thought uniquely human, scene-memory now has a feathered precedent.

term: 忘了‘学过’，却仍会做
oneLiner: 失忆病人再握到那只‘会刺痛’的手，会缩手却说不清为哪般。
oneLinerEn: An amnesic recoils again from the hand that pinched, yet cannot say why.
detail: 克拉帕雷德给一位严重失忆者握手时藏一枚针刺，她痛得缩手；再见此人却完全不记得。但她的身体‘记得’：她抗拒再握这只手，却给不出理由。显性记忆（能说出）与隐性记忆（会做）是两套系统。你以为的‘忘了’，很多时候只是忘了‘记得’。
detailEn: Claparède pricked an amnesic's palm with a hidden pin during a handshake; she recoiled, and next moment remembered nothing. Yet her body kept the lesson: she balked at the hand, without a reason. Explicit and implicit memory are separate systems; to have 'forgotten' is often only to have forgotten that you remember.

term: 超忆症：无法忘记的自传体记忆
oneLiner: 有人能背出三年前某天吃了啥、星期几，却毫无窍门。
oneLinerEn: Some can recall what they ate on a day three years past and the weekday, with no technique.
detail: 帕克等人报告了首批被确认的‘超忆症’者：他们能异常准确地说出过去具体某日的经历，但这并非主动苦练，而是一种拦不住、自动涌来的记忆。记忆并非越‘强’越好的简单加法：它伴随负荷，也难以删掉不想要的部分。‘遗忘’也许不只是失败，而是大脑一项必要的编辑功能。
detailEn: Parker and colleagues reported the first confirmed cases: people who name what happened on a past date with startling accuracy, not by practice but by memory they cannot stem. Total recall is not an unalloyed gift—it carries load and resists deletion, hinting that forgetting is a vital editor, not a mere failure.

term: 舌尖现象：就在嘴边，却说不出
oneLiner: 你知道那个词、知道首字母、就是怎么也拿不出来。
oneLinerEn: You know the word, its first letter, everything—yet cannot get it out.
detail: 布朗与麦克尼尔系统描述了这种『话到嘴边又卡住』：你能说出目标词的部分信息（音节数、首字母），却提取不到完整形式。这说明‘知道一个词’并不是一块，而是语义、音韵、拼写等多模块分别存储，任何一个都可能单独‘卡壳’。‘忘了’有时不是丢失，而是暂时接不上那个标签。
detailEn: Brown and McNeill described the state where you hold a word's outline—its first letter, its length—yet not the whole. 'Knowing a word' is not one bit but separate stores of meaning, sound and spelling, any of which can jam alone. Forgetting here is not loss but the label failing to connect.

term: Bouba/Kiki：声音自带形状
oneLiner: 把‘bouba’和‘kiki’分给圆块和尖刺，几乎全世界都分对。
oneLinerEn: Assign 'bouba' and 'kiki' to a blob and a spike, and nearly everyone agrees.
detail: 克尔勒与后来的拉马钱德兰都发现，面对一个圆滚和一个尖刺的图形，绝大多数人把软软的音配给圆的、把尖硬的音配给刺，跨语言、跨文化都高度一致。这说明声音与形状之间并非全然是任意的约定，大脑能跨感官地读出某种‘共同形状’。语言的地基里，也许藏着几分先天的联觉。
detailEn: Köhler, and later Ramachandran, found that people pair round sounds with the blob and spiky sounds with the star, across tongues and cultures. Sound and shape are not wholly arbitrary convention; the brain reads a shared contour across senses. A little innate synaesthesia may lie in language's foundations.

term: 加工层次：靠‘想得深’而非‘看得久’记住
oneLiner: 决定你能否记住的，不是重复几次，而是你有多深地想过它。
oneLinerEn: What you keep depends not on repetition but on how deeply you thought it.
detail: 克雷克与洛克哈特让被试对同一批词做不同深度的判断：看字形、听韵律、还是想意思。结果，仅仅‘想过含义’的词记得远好于只看外表的词，而与花多少时间无关。记忆是加工深度的副产品：与已有知识连接得越多，扎得越深。‘背不牢’常常不是没花够时间，而是没想够深度。
detailEn: Craik and Lockhart had people judge words by shape, rhyme or meaning; those merely pondered for sense outlasted surface looks, regardless of time spent. Memory is a by-product of depth: the more it links to what you know, the deeper it roots. Poor recall is often not too little time but too little thought.

term: 倒脸效应：颠倒的脸突然认不出
oneLiner: 同样一张熟脸，一旦倒过来就难认得多，别的物体却没那么糟。
oneLinerEn: Turn a known face upside-down and recognition collapses—objects fare far less badly.
detail: 殷发现，颠倒会让辨认面孔变得尤其困难，而这种‘怕颠倒’在房子、汽车等其他物体上要弱得多。这被视为证据：面孔并非靠零散部件识别，而是靠一套专门处理‘整体关系’的机制，一倒过来就被打断。认脸看似人人都会，背后却是一套专门、脆弱而精妙的硬件。
detailEn: Yin showed inversion cripples face recognition far more than it does for houses or cars. This is read as evidence that faces are seen not by parts but by a configural mechanism, broken when turned upside-down. Recognising a face looks effortless but runs on specialised, fragile, exquisite hardware.

term: 出丑效应：完美的人打翻咖啡更可爱
oneLiner: 能力出众者犯个小错，人缘反而上升；平庸者出丑只会更扣分。
oneLinerEn: A small blunder makes the talented likelier to be liked, the mediocre less so.
detail: 阿伦森让受试听一段答题录音：一个几近完美的候选人，和一个同样优秀却在结尾不小心打翻咖啡的人——后者更讨人喜欢。恰到好处的瑕疵把人从‘神’拉回‘人’。但这份好感只对已经优秀的人生效，完美若本不存在，犯错只是雪上加霜。
detailEn: Aronson had people hear a near-flawless quiz contestant, and the same one who knocks over coffee at the end—the blunderer was liked more. A small flaw pulls 'god' back to 'human'. The charm only works on the already-capable; for everyone else a blunder just compounds.

term: 变色龙效应：我们不由自主地模仿
oneLiner: 你会悄悄学对面那人的姿势与口头禅，对方也因此更对你有好感。
oneLinerEn: You mirroring the other's posture and phrases unbidden—and they like you for it.
detail: 查兰特与巴奇发现，人们会无意识地模仿交谈对象的摸脸、撑腮、语速，且完全察觉不到；被同步模仿的人反而觉得对方更讨人喜欢。社会亲和很大一部分是在身体层面默默同步完成的。‘我们很像’的亲密感，有时是我们先无意识地把自己变成了对方的样子。
detailEn: Chartrand and Bargh found people mirror a partner's face-touching, slouching and pace without noticing, and those mirrored like them more. Much social rapport is silently synchronised at the body's level; the sense 'we're alike' often comes from unknowingly becoming the other's shape.

term: 社会比较：自我评价其实来自‘和谁比’
oneLiner: 同一份成绩，因周围参照不同，会感到‘很糟’或‘不错’。
oneLinerEn: The same result feels awful or fine depending on who is nearby to compare with.
detail: 费斯廷格提出，人在缺乏客观标准时，会靠与他人比较来评价自己的能力与观点。‘大鱼小塘’效应印证了这点：同样的学生，在尖子班自我能力感反而更低。我们的自信、不满、抱负，很大程度不是对世界的直接读数，而是对所选参照系的读数。
detailEn: Festinger held that absent objective standards we judge ability and opinion by comparing with others. The 'big-fish-little-pond' effect bears it out: the same student feels less able among stars. Confidence and discontent are often a reading not of the world but of the chosen reference group.

term: 得寸进尺：先应小忙，就易应大请
oneLiner: 答应了一个小请求，之后答应同主题大请求的概率飙升。
oneLinerEn: Say yes to a small ask and you're far likelier to say yes to the big one.
detail: 弗里德曼与弗雷泽让住户先挂一块小标语、几周后再请他们在草坪立一块巨大丑陋的广告牌——先应下小的那组，答应大的比例高出一大截。为了保持一个连贯的‘我是这种人’的自我形象，我们会顺着先前的‘是’继续。小的同意，常常是通向大的那扇门。
detailEn: Freedman and Fraser asked homeowners to display a tiny sign, then weeks later to plant a huge ugly billboard; those who'd agreed small agreed far more often. To stay coherent with 'the kind of person I am', we follow an earlier yes. The small concession is often the doorway to the large.

term: 以退为进：先被拒大，再应小成
oneLiner: 先抛一个离谱大要求让你拒，再退一小步，你就更容易点头。
oneLinerEn: Start with an absurd ask you refuse, retreat to a modest one, and yes becomes likelier.
detail: 恰尔迪尼等发现，先请学生做两年义务辅导（几乎人人拒绝），再请带少管所孩子逛一次动物园，答应率远高于直接只提后者。退让被视为一种‘让步’，触发互惠；那个大请求还顺带当了一次‘锚’。说服常常不在内容里，而在它如何安排了先后。
detailEn: Cialdini and colleagues asked students for two years of tutoring (all refuse), then one zoo trip with kids; acceptance jumped versus asking the trip alone. The retreat reads as concession and triggers reciprocity, while the huge first ask sets an anchor. Persuasion often lives not in the content but in the ordering.

term: 心流：最好的体验来自‘忘了自己’
oneLiner: 最投入、最快乐时，那个‘我在干嘛’的监视声反而消失了。
oneLinerEn: At peak engagement the inner narrator 'what am I doing' goes quiet.
detail: 契凯森特米哈伊描述，当挑战与技能恰到好处匹配、目标清晰、反馈即时，人会进入一种自我感消退、时间感扭曲、行动与意识融为一体的高度专注。它提示：幸福未必来自放松，而常来自‘把难度调到刚好’的专注。过度自我监控反而会打断这份心流。
detailEn: Csikszentmihalyi described a state where challenge and skill meet with clear goals and instant feedback: self-awareness fades, time warps, action and awareness merge. Well-being comes less from ease than from difficulty tuned just right. Excessive self-monitoring is what breaks the spell.

term: 情绪传染：表情会把你‘带入’那种心情
oneLiner: 模仿别人的面部表情，会让你的情绪真的朝它靠过去。
oneLinerEn: Mimic another's face and your mood quietly drifts toward theirs.
detail: 哈特菲尔德等提出‘自动反馈’链条：我们会不由自主地微模仿他人表情，面部反馈再把这份表情对应的感受带回给自己。于是他人的焦虑、热情会像涟漪一样越过个体边界。结合‘情绪建构’，这更说明情绪不只是在自己脑内发生的事——它常常被他人‘写’进你的身体。
detailEn: Hatfield and colleagues traced an automatic loop: we subtly mimic another's expression, and facial feedback returns its feeling to us. So anxiety and enthusiasm cross the border of the self. With constructed emotion, this shows feeling is not made only inside your skull; others write it into your body.

term: 过度自信：能力判断里那道系统偏差
oneLiner: 绝大多数司机都自认技术高于平均水平——数学上不可能。
oneLinerEn: Most drivers rate themselves above average—which is arithmetically impossible.
detail: 穆尔与希利梳理出三种过度自信：过高估计（认为自己做得比实际好）、过高定位（认为自己比同侪强）、过高精确（对答案把握超过应有的把握）。它们在很多领域稳健重现。自信与能力的相关往往很弱：那份‘我拿准了’的笃定，常常只是感觉，而非证据。
detailEn: Moore and Healy separated overestimation, overplacement (better than peers) and overprecision (too sure). They recur across domains; confidence correlates weakly with ability. The steady 'I've got this' is often a feeling rather than evidence.

term: 真相错觉：重复让谎言更像真的
oneLiner: 同一句话听得多，你就更觉得它真，无关它是否属实。
oneLinerEn: Hear a claim often and it feels truer, whether or not it is.
detail: 哈舍等让受试反复对一些陌生陈述打‘真假’分，几天内重复越多，被判定为‘真’的越多——哪怕毫无新证据。熟悉感会被误读成真实感，因为‘想不起来出处却异常熟悉’的句子读起来毫不费力。这正是谣言与宣传反复轰炸后起效的深层机制。
detailEn: Hasher and colleagues had people rate unfamiliar statements true or false across days; repeated items were judged truer with no new evidence. Familiarity is misread as truth, because what comes to mind smoothly feels right. This is the engine behind propaganda and the spread of claims.

term: 生成效应：自己产出答案更记得
oneLiner: 比起看现成答案，自己费力给出的词，日后记得更牢。
oneLinerEn: A word you produced yourself is remembered better than one you were shown.
detail: 斯拉梅卡与格拉夫发现，让人自己填出配对词（哪怕只是猜），比直接读到那对词，之后的回忆成绩明显更好。自己生成的信息更深地接入原有知识网络，留下了更多日后能‘找回来’的路径。被动接收看似省力，却常常是记得最差的一种。
detailEn: Slamecka and Graf found that producing a word oneself—even guessing—beats being shown the pair for later recall. Self-generated items weave into existing knowledge and leave more routes back. Passive intake feels easy yet is often the least well remembered.

term: 巴纳姆效应：为‘万能评语’对号入座
oneLiner: 一段放之四海皆准的模糊描述，人人都觉得‘这说的就是我’。
oneLinerEn: Vague lines true of almost anyone feel uncannily personal to each reader.
detail: 费勒给学生一份据称是‘个性化测评’的人格报告，实为同一段话复制给所有人；多数人却认为它精准得惊人。人类极擅长把抽象、两可的描述主动解读成关于自己的细节。这解释了星座、算命、许多网络‘人格测试’为何总能戳中你——是你在替它完成精确。
detailEn: Forer gave students a supposedly individual personality readout that was one generic paragraph handed to everyone; most found it eerily apt. We readily recast vague, two-sided claims as about us. It explains why horoscopes and online quizzes land—because you supply the precision.

term: 蔡格尼克效应：未完之事更挂怀
oneLiner: 没做完的事在记忆里盘旋，做完的反而很快被放下。
oneLinerEn: Unfinished tasks hover in memory while completed ones slip away.
detail: 蔡格尼克观察到服务员对未结账的订单记得清清楚楚，一结完账就忘得一干二净。实验也显示人们对被打断、未完成的工作回忆得更牢。未完成的紧张会保持一份‘后台待办’持续在线。这既是拖延的折磨来源，也是‘先开工五分钟’能破局的机制。
detailEn: Zeigarnik saw waiters hold unpaid orders in perfect memory, then lose them once settled, and experiments echo it: interrupted, unfinished work is recalled better. Uncompletion keeps a background to-do live—for both the torment of a lingering task and the reason five minutes of starting helps.

term: 「历史的终结」错觉：以为现在的自己是成品
oneLiner: 我们承认十年前的自己很陌生，却相信现在的我几乎不会再变。
oneLinerEn: We grant we were alien a decade ago yet insist the present me is basically final.
detail: 夸伊德巴赫等发现，人们能看清过去的自己在价值观、挚爱、性格上巨变，却笃信未来的自己会大致保持现状，于是愿意花大钱去保住‘现在的喜好’。每个当下都像站在历史的终点。这份错觉让人低估了未来自我的变化，也为拖延、为对‘永远的我’的执念埋下伏笔。
detailEn: Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson found people see their past selves as transformed in values, tastes and traits yet insist future selves will barely change, so they pay to preserve today's likes. Each present feels like history's end—underpricing the person you'll become and tempting delay.

term: 来源监控：分不清‘听过’还是‘想过’
oneLiner: 大脑会把生动想象的事，事后当成自己真的经历过。
oneLinerEn: Vividly imagined events can later be filed as things that really happened.
detail: 约翰逊与雷指出，我们判定一段记忆来自现实还是想象，靠的是内容特征（细节、情绪、感官强度）。可一旦想象得足够生动，就与真实知觉难分彼此，于是产生‘来源错配’：编过的故事、听来的说法，事后被当成亲身的记忆。这与‘确信感可被制造’一起，揭开了‘我记得=发生过’这层假设。
detailEn: Johnson and Raye argued we tag a memory as real or imagined by its features—detail, emotion, sensory richness. Vivid imagination then rivals perception, so sources misfile: invented or heard claims get booked as lived memory. Together with manufactured confidence it loosens the equation 'remembered = happened'.

term: 当下偏差：为‘现在就爽’不惜代价
oneLiner: 同样的等待，若收益在眼前，估值就远超在遥远的未来。
oneLinerEn: The same delay is priced far dearer when the reward sits right now.
detail: 弗雷德里克等梳理出‘双曲贴现’：我们对即时满足的偏好远超理性一致——今天要多等一周觉得无所谓，但从‘今天吃一块’到‘明天吃两块’却难以自持。这会催生反复改口的计划与拖延。我们并非不懂长远，而是每逢选择路口，当下的诱惑总会插队。
detailEn: Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue charted hyperbolic discounting: we overweight the immediate—in a week's wait feels trivial, yet today-vs-tomorrow is hard to bear. This breeds rescheduled plans and delay. We do grasp the long run; we keep failing the moment it's on the table.

term: 玫瑰色回忆：过去被回看得比当时更美
oneLiner: 同一段假期，事后回忆比当时体验打的分更高。
oneLinerEn: The same trip is rated higher in retrospect than in the moment.
detail: 米切尔等人在假期前后追踪游客的实时感受与事后回忆，发现回忆普遍比现场体验更正面，负面情绪被选择性淡化。回忆不是对过去的忠实重播，而是一位爱美的剪辑师。这也为‘怀旧’与‘过去总比现在好’的错觉埋下伏笔：你怀念的，未必真那样好。
detailEn: Mitchell and colleagues tracked vacationers' moment-to-moment feelings and later recall: retrospect rated higher, negatives thinned. Memory is not a faithful replay but an flattering editor—feeding the illusion that the past was better than the present, since what you miss may never have been so good.

term: 超纠正：自信的错最难忘改
oneLiner: 越是自信满满地答错，纠正后反而越容易重踏覆辙。
oneLinerEn: High-confidence wrong answers, once corrected, prove hardest to fix.
detail: 巴特菲尔德与梅特卡夫发现，人们对‘高置信度的错误’在得知正解后，下次仍更易重错，而对低置信的错误反而容易纠正。强烈的自信会让大脑在纠错时低估意外，既不更新也不长记性。它把‘确信’的代价摆上台面：那份笃定不仅掩盖了错，还阻碍了改。
detailEn: Butterfield and Metcalfe found that high-confidence errors, once corrected, recur more than low-confidence ones: strong certainty makes the brain under-weigh the surprise of being wrong, so it neither updates nor learns. The cost of confidence is shown plainly—it hides the error and blocks its repair.

term: 情境依赖记忆：换个房间，就想不起来
oneLiner: 在同一间屋子里学、同一间屋子里考，成绩会更好；离开就卡壳。
oneLinerEn: Learn and test in the same room and you do better; leave it and you falter.
detail: 戈登等让潜水员在岸上或水底背词表，再在相同或不同环境里考：编码与提取环境一致时回忆明显更好。环境中的气味、声音、姿态都在无形中为记忆打了标签。所谓‘忘了’，有时不是丢，而是缺少了当初那把开锁的情境钥匙。
detailEn: Godden and Baddeley had divers learn word lists on shore or underwater and recall best when context matched at test. Room smells, sounds and posture quietly tag memory. 'Forgetting' is sometimes not loss but the missing context-key that unlocked it.

term: 内群体共情偏差：对他人的痛，反肤不均
oneLiner: 看到同肤色的人受苦，大脑的‘疼痛回路’反腅得更强烈。
oneLinerEn: The brain's pain circuits resonate more for a same-race face in agony.
detail: 韩等用功能成像发现，受试看到与自己同族面孔遭受疼痛时，共情相关脑区反应强于看异族面孔受苦。共情并非均匀洒向所有人，而会被‘我们/他们’的分类调节。这提醒我们：‘感同身受’并非天生普适，而需要刻意拓宽它的圈。
detailEn: Han and colleagues found stronger empathy-related brain responses to a same-race face in pain than an other-race one. Empathy is not evenly poured but tuned by 'us/them'. A caution that felt-shared feeling is not born universal and must be deliberately widened.

term: 脸盲者把面孔当物体认
oneLiner: 认不出脸的病人，靠辨认物体那套系统也能勉强‘认’出一张张面孔。
oneLinerEn: A face-blind patient can still 'read' faces by leaning on object-recognition systems.
detail: 拉杜与杜邦斯报告了一位先天脸盲者：她无法走那条‘看脸专楼’，却练就了用物体识别的方式分析五官，靠策略性拼凑完成辨认。这说明大脑的分工不是一成不变：一条路断了，另一条能绕行。‘认人’这种看似本能的能力，也可以被重新编译。
detailEn: Duchaine reported a congenital prosopagnosic who, barred from the dedicated face route, trained herself to analyse features as objects and assemble recognition strategically. The brain's divisions are not rigid; when one road fails, another detours. Even 'knowing a face' can be recompiled.

term: 心理练习：想象也是一次练习
oneLiner: 只在脑中反复‘想象’一个动作或声音，也能让真实辨认变得更快更准。
oneLinerEn: Merely rehearsing an act or sound in the mind sharpens real-world performance.
detail: 从想象练习钢琴到想象运动，神经影像显示它在很大程度上激活了与实际执行交叠的脑区，并真能提升后续表现。大脑的‘模拟’与‘实演’之间并非泾渭分明。心象训练之所以有效，因为对大脑而言，生动的想象本身就是一次准经验。
detailEn: From imagined piano to imagined sport, imagery lights much the same regions as doing and measurably improves later performance. The mind's simulation and enactment are not cleanly divided. Mental practice works because vivid imagining is, to the brain, a kind of experience.

term: 时间错位：现在正悄悄改写刚才
oneLiner: 随后发生的事，会让你把刚才那一刻的时间往它那边‘拉近’。
oneLinerEn: What follows silently drags the just-past moment closer to it in time.
detail: 现在知觉到事件之后，人们对‘它发生在何时’的回测会被后续事件拉拢，两个靠得很近的事会在记忆中互相靠拢。大脑并不把时间当成一个客观容器来记账，而是根据因果与关联重新编排。你以为的‘时间线’，其实是事后被整理过的叙事。
detailEn: After an event, people's back-timing of it is pulled toward a later event; two close happenings draw together in memory. The brain does not keep time as an objective ledger but reorders it by cause and link. Your felt 'timeline' is a story tidied after the fact.

term: 专家也常错：自信不等于准确率
oneLiner: 在‘ wicked’领域里，专家的预测自信几乎不反映对错。
oneLinerEn: In 'wicked' environments, expert confidence barely tracks correctness.
detail: 特洛克梳理出判断的两类环境：在‘友善’（规律稳定、反馈即时，如国际象棋）里，自信能反映准确率；在‘ wicked ’（开放、反馈模糊，如政治预测）里，两者几乎脱钩。专家的光环常常只是把领域错选。它提醒：同一个人的自信，在不同领域里的含金量截然不同。
detailEn: Tetlock split judgment into kind and wicked environments: in kind ones (chess) confidence tracks accuracy; in wicked ones (political forecasting) the two come apart, and the expert halo is often a domain chosen badly. One person's confidence is worth very different sums in different fields.

term: 偏好会改写你的第一眼
oneLiner: 还没‘决定’，你的眼睛已先多睜那些你更可能选的东西。
oneLinerEn: Before you choose, your eyes already linger on what you'll pick.
detail: 眼动显示，我们在浏览选项时，目光会不自觉地多落在最终选中的那些上。看似‘理性权衡’之后才有的偏好，其实从第一瞥就被摆渡。注意、偏好与选择在毫秒间相互喂养。你以为‘看了一圈才选’，不如说‘一边看一边已经被引导着选’。
detailEn: Eye-tracking shows gaze drifts toward the items we end up choosing while we scan. Preference thought to follow deliberation is steered from the first look. Attention, preference and choice feed one another in milliseconds—you did not survey then pick; you were picking as you looked.

term: 习惯一旦形塑，目标消失它仍运行
oneLiner: 那个行为早不再给你想要的奖偿，你仍会沿旧线索去做。
oneLinerEn: The act no longer pays, yet you still run it off the old cue.
detail: 杜利等训练大鼠按‘目标降解’去压杆，一旦把某个动作变成习惯，就算撤走它原本的奖赏、甚至事先告知‘今天没奖’，它们仍会去做。习惯被‘线索’而非‘目标’驱动，存在另一套不经过当下欲望的回路。这解释了为何明知无益，旧习惯仍会在特定情境自动开火。
detailEn: After training rats to press for a goal, once an action became habitual it survived the goal's removal—even when the reward was taken away beforehand, they still pressed. Habit is cue-driven and rides a circuit that bypasses present desire. It shows why an old routine fires on cue despite its pointlessness.

term: 后天涌现的学者综合征
oneLiner: 少数人在一场脑伤或痴果后，忽然展现出惊人的艺术或数学才能。
oneLinerEn: After some injuries or dementia, startling artistic or numeric gifts appear.
detail: 一些原本普通的患者在特定脑区受损或退化后，突然涌现绘画、音乐或计算方面的过人能力。一种解释是受损区域对下游的‘抑制’解除，被长期压住的能力得以释放。它提示：大脑的潜能或许部分被‘闸门’锁着，天赋未必只是添加，也可能是去抑制。
detailEn: A few previously ordinary patients, after damage or degeneration in certain areas, burst into prodigious drawing, music or calculation. One account: the injured region stops inhibiting what lies downstream, releasing a buried capacity. Talent may be as much disinhibition as addition.

term: 一瞥定信任：0.1秒就评好了陌生人
oneLiner: 只看一张陌生脸十分之一秒，你就已判定了他‘可信与否’。
oneLinerEn: A tenth of a second on a strange face is enough to rate its trustworthiness.
detail: 威里斯与扎格塔发现，让人极短暂地看政治候选人的面孔后判断能力与可信度，仅凭一瞥得出的结论与看很久的结论高度相关，且能部分预测选举结果。社会判断在意识来得及参与前就已启动。‘第一印象’不只是一个比喻，它几乎是一个硬编码的即时读数。
detailEn: Todorov showed that rating competence and trust from faces flashed for a tenth of a second tracks judgments made with long viewing and even predicts elections partly. Social read-out fires before awareness can weigh in. 'First impressions' is not a metaphor but a near-hard-coded instant reading.

term: 情绪窄化记忆：记住中心，丢掉背景
oneLiner: 情绪事件让核心细节记得更牢，却让周围细节反而更差。
oneLinerEn: Emotion buries the gist in memory while the surroundings slip away.
detail: 克里斯坦迪万迪斯等提出‘情绪视觉注意窄化’：令人激愤的画面会像聚光灯把注意收到中心，中心记得更牢、周围却记得更少。情绪不是给整幕录像加清晰度，而是把光打在一点。这解释了为何见证者能详述枪、却说不清凶手的衣着。
detailEn: Christiaans & Murre proposed emotional cuing narrows visual attention: arousing pictures spotlight the centre, improving it while degrading the surround. Emotion does not sharpen the whole scene; it aims a beam. It shows why a witness can detail the gun yet miss the clothing.

term: 风险直觉来自情绪而非算术
oneLiner: 对危险的判断，常由胸中那阵‘不对劲’而非概率表决定。
oneLinerEn: Risk is judged by a gut 'something's wrong', not a probability table.
detail: 西科洛等提出‘风险即感受’：人们对某事危不危险的直觉，与它的客观统计风险常常脱节，却与它唤起的情绪强度高度相关。同一个数字，换个描述、换个心情，就判然不同。我们自认在算风险，其实多半是在读自己身体递上来的那份情绪分数。
detailEn: Slovic and colleagues held that felt risk tracks the emotion a thing stirs rather than its statistics. The same figure, reframed or felt differently, is judged apart. We think we compute risk while mostly reading the feeling-score the body hands up.

term: 你看到的，部分是被你‘认出’的
oneLiner: 同一个墨迹，被‘命名’为不同东西后，你看它的方式真的变了。
oneLinerEn: Name the same blot as different things and how you see it genuinely shifts.
detail: 先给受试一个物体名称，再让他在噪声中辨认，他的知觉会朝那个名称偏移；同样一幅图，被标为‘动物’还是‘工具’，会影响之后对细节的记忆与分类。辨认不只是由视网膜往上传，也受高层次的‘知道它是什么’往下灌注。我们以为客观的‘一眼看出’，其实早被概念与期待渗透。
detailEn: Prime an object's name and later identification in noise drifts toward it; label the same drawing 'animal' or 'tool' and it bends later memory and sorting. Seeing is not only bottom-up from the retina but suffused with top-down knowledge of what it is. The 'plain look' we trust is already soaked in concept and expectation.

term: 语言相对论：母语是一把切世界的刀
oneLiner: 语言未必限制你能想什么，却习惯性地引导你总往某些方向想。
oneLinerEn: Language may not cap what you can think, but it habituates which distinctions you tend to draw.
detail: 「萨丕尔-沃尔夫假说」的强硬版——语言决定思维——早已被推翻，但一个温和版本获得了不少证据支持。不同语言强迫你在说话前先记下不同的信息：有的必须标明时态、有的必须分单复数、有的必须写清东南西北。这些被迫养成的习惯，会微妙地影响说话人对时间、颜色、空间与因果的默认切分。语言不是思想的牢笼，而更像一副反复替你磨好的眼镜。
detailEn: The strong Whorf claim that language caps thought has long been rejected, but a softer version has gathered real support. Different tongues force speakers to log different facts before a sentence can be uttered: tense, number, or cardinal direction must be marked. These trained habits subtly tilt how speakers default to carving time, colour, space and cause. Language is less a cage than a pair of well-worn glasses you keep looking through.

term: 语法性别：让桥更「美」还是更「强」
oneLiner: 同一个「桥」，在阴性语言里被形容得更柔美，在阳性语言里更雄壮。
oneLinerEn: The very same 'bridge' sounds slimmer and more elegant in one language than another.
detail: 德语的「桥」是阴性，西班牙语却是阳性。博罗季茨基等人让两组人形容一座桥，德语使用者更多说「美丽、优雅、纤细」，西语使用者更多说「强壮、坚固、高大」。更微妙的是，当被要求给一个从未见过的新词分类时，语法性别会悄悄牵引受试的直觉。语法里那些看似空洞的「性」，竟在形容无生命之物时被重新激活，渗进我们的想象。
detailEn: 'Bridge' is feminine in German but masculine in Spanish. Asked to describe a bridge, German speakers leaned toward 'beautiful, elegant, slender' while Spanish speakers said 'strong, sturdy, towering'. Grammatical gender even nudged intuitions when people sorted novel words. An apparently empty category in grammar gets reawakened when we talk about lifeless objects.

term: 活在你的坐标系里：方位语言塑造记忆
oneLiner: 有的语言不用「左右」，只用东南西北——说这种话的人，方向感惊人。
oneLinerEn: Languages without 'left/right' but only compass bearings seem to rewire speakers' sense of orientation.
detail: 澳洲原住的Guugu Yimithirr语几乎没有「左/右」的说法，日常方位一律用「北/南/东/西」表达。说话人必须随时知道自己面朝何方，也因此在任何环境中都能瞬间指出正北。博罗季茨基的实验发现：让他们在桌面上摆放一系列卡片时，会不自觉沿某个地理轴向排列，且这一排列与母语习惯相关。你以为中性的「空间感」，原来是母语每天训练几十遍的产物。
detailEn: Guugu Yimithirr of Australia barely uses 'left/right'; it speaks daily life in compass bearings. Speakers must track their facing at every moment, so they can point to true north in any room. Boroditsky found that when they arrange cards, the line drifts along a geographic axis tied to the mother tongue. What feels like a neutral 'sense of space' turns out to be trained dozens of times a day by grammar.

term: 换个隐喻，换个政策：犯罪是野兽还是病毒？
oneLiner: 同样一组犯罪数据，把罪比喻成「野兽」或「病毒」，人们偏好的政策就跟着换。
oneLinerEn: Describe crime as a 'beast' or a 'virus' and readers back different policies without noticing.
detail: 提布多与博罗季茨基给读者呈现同一份关于犯罪的报道，唯一的差别是比喻：一个版本说「犯罪是这座城市的野兽」，另一个说「犯罪是病毒」。读完之后，被「野兽」框架启动的读者更倾向加强警力，被「病毒」启动的读者更倾向社会治理与投资。妙的是，受试大多否认这些句子影响了他们。隐喻不只是修辞装饰，它偷偷把问题的解决路径也一起打包送了进来。
detailEn: Thibodeau and Boroditsky handed readers the same statistics, framed only as 'crime is a beast ravaging the city' or 'crime is a virus infecting the city'. Readers leaned toward more policing in the beast frame and more social investment in the virus frame, while insisting the wording had not swayed them. Metaphor is not decoration; it quietly delivers a solution set with the problem.

term: 一个动词的结构，决定你记住谁在做
oneLiner: 「她打碎了花瓶」和「花瓶碎了」，让你对同一件事的追责与记忆都不同。
oneLinerEn: 'She broke the vase' vs 'the vase broke' changes who you remember and who you blame.
detail: 英语有及物（她打碎了花瓶）和不及物（花瓶碎了）两套说法。福西与博罗季茨基发现，看同样的意外视频，听到及物句的人更容易记住「是谁做的」，也更倾向追责；听到不及物句的人则更少关注施事者，即使视频里明显有人在操作。西班牙语、日语里不及物用法更常见，母语者对「谁是主角」的记忆也随之不同。语法并非对世界的中性转录，它更像一位剪辑师，决定镜头停在哪。
detailEn: English lets you say 'she broke the vase' or the agentless 'the vase broke'. Fausey and Boroditsky showed that after watching the same accident, people who heard the transitive line remembered the agent better and assigned more blame; the intransitive line drew less attention to the doer, even when one was clearly present. Languages that favour intransitive framing seem to yield speakers who notice agency a little differently. Grammar is an editor, not a neutral transcript.

term: 没有精确数词的语言，人怎么数数
oneLiner: 语言里没有「7」「8」这些词时，成年人也难做精确区分。
oneLinerEn: Without words for exact numbers, even adults struggle to tell seven from eight.
detail: 亚马逊的Munduruku语只有到「5」左右的精确数词，更大的数字只靠近似。弗兰克等人让他们比较两组圆点，结果发现：只要数量超过「4」，他们的判断就退化为「大概谁多谁少」。同一批人若搬到城市、学会葡萄牙语，精确计数能力会显著回升。这条证据说明：人类天生拥有「近似数量系统」，但「精确到个位数」的直觉，是把数词表装进大脑之后才点亮的能力。
detailEn: The Munduruká language of the Amazon has exact words only up to around 'five'; larger numbers rely on approximation. Frank and colleagues asked speakers to compare dot arrays: past about four, judgements collapsed to 'roughly who has more'. The same people, once they learned Portuguese in a city setting, gained exact-counting skill. Humans seem born with an approximate number system, and precise enumeration arrives only once number words are installed.

term: 情绪颗粒度：能叫得出名字，才管得住它
oneLiner: 能区分「恼怒、委屈、沮丧」的人，比只会说「不爽」的人更擅长调节情绪。
oneLinerEn: Naming 'irritation, letdown, wistfulness' beats a vague 'bad mood' for regulation.
detail: 巴雷特等人提出「情绪粒度」概念：一个人把内感受切分成具体情绪类别的能力。她让受试看一段引发不适的影像，随后测量情绪恢复速度。结果发现，能精确命名自己状态的人（如「失望」而非笼统的「难受」）恢复得更快，也较少依赖酗酒等替代方式。语言在这里不是给已有的情绪贴标签，而是参与制造了情绪本身——越精细的词汇，越像一组精准的小钥匙。
detailEn: Barrett's group coined 'emotional granularity': how finely you carve bodily arousal into distinct feelings. People who could label a state precisely — 'letdown' rather than a vague 'bad mood' recovered faster from unpleasant films and leaned less on alcohol. Language here is not merely tagging pre-built emotions; it helps construct them. A finer vocabulary behaves like a set of small precise keys.

term: 数词越短，你能记住的越多
oneLiner: 数字发音占用时间越长，短时记忆容量越小。
oneLinerEn: The longer number words take to say, the fewer you can hold.
detail: 工作记忆里的数字广度并非由「智力」单独决定，而是受发音长度影响。塞尔维斯发现：说威尔士语的人数字广度偏小，因为它们的音节多、发音慢；而中文数字几乎都可以在四分之一个音节内说出来，因此中文母语者的数字广度往往更大。把「复述速度」人为加速后，这个差距也会缩小。语言对记忆的帮助，藏在它「能不能在心里悄悄快速念出来」里。
detailEn: Working-memory digit span is bounded less by raw intelligence than by how long each number takes to say. Service showed Welsh speakers had smaller spans because their words are syllabically heavy; Chinese digits are pronounced in one quick beat, and speakers gain a larger span. Compressing the pronunciation closed the gap. Language helps memory when it lets you sub-vocalise numbers fast.

term: 内心独白：那个「自言自语」其实是在「说」
oneLiner: 你脑中的那个声音，是有内容的、偶尔多人的，也可能根本不存在。
oneLinerEn: The voice in your head has content, sometimes multiple, and sometimes it is entirely absent.
detail: 胡尔伯特用随机蜂鸣提示法采样人们当下的心智内容，发现「内心言语」比传统教科书描述的要稀少得多：只有一部分人频繁体验它，而且它不像默读那样连续，常常是片段、半句、甚至不是自己的声音。另一些人则几乎没有内心语言，只在「想到」而非「说出」。这个看似私密的普遍现象，其实个体差异极大。语言不只是我们对外的工具，也可能构成「思考」本身的一种可选择的模式。
detailEn: Sampling minds with random beeps, Hurlburt found inner speech far rarer than textbooks suggest: only some people experience it often, and it is fragmentary, sometimes not even their own voice. Others think with almost no verbal stream at all. The supposedly universal phenomenon shows enormous individual variation. Language may be not just an outward tool but an optional mode in which thinking can run.

term: 年龄越大，一年越短
termEn: Time Seems to Speed Up With Age
oneLiner: 一年在你生命中占比越来越小，于是主观上，它也越过越快。
oneLinerEn: Each year shrinks as a share of your life, and subjectively it starts to flash by.
detail: 十岁的一年是你已活过时光的全部；四十岁的一年，只是其中的四分之一。这条从十九世纪就被反复提及的「比例理论」，可以解释为什么长大后的假期、学期、季节似乎一部比一部短。另一个补充解释是「新异事件密度」：年轻时充了太多第一次，回忆里被拉得很长；成年后日子同构重复，往回看就像被压成短短一格。
detailEn: At ten, a year is your entire life so far; at forty, only a quarter of it. This proportional account explains why school breaks and seasons seem to shrink after childhood. A companion is novelty density: youth is packed with first times, stretching memory backward, while adult days blur together into one compressed retrospect.

term: 我们记的不是时长，而是「峰值+结尾」
oneLiner: 一段体验持续多久，几乎不影响你事后对它的评分。
oneLinerEn: How long an experience lasts barely changes how you later rate it.
detail: 卡尼曼等人让受试分别接受短一点和长一点的不适水浸（长度不同、但结尾相同），他们事后对两段体验的「不喜欢程度」几乎一样，只根据峰值与结尾如何收场来评判。这个发现被称为「持续时长忽视」。我们以为自己在衡量一件事“过了多久”，其实大脑记账时用的是“感受多强、如何收尾”这两个样本，而非时长本身。
detailEn: Kahneman's team gave people short and long versions of an unpleasant cold-water soak that shared the same ending. Later dislike ratings barely differed — they tracked the peak and how the episode ended, not its length. Duration neglect shows that remembered experience is sampled at peaks and endings, not metered in real time.

term: 新奇的一刻，时间会被拉长
oneLiner: 意外出现的那个刺激，在主观上会比实际持续得更久。
oneLinerEn: The unexpected, novel event seems to stretch longer than it actually lasts.
detail: 在一串完全相同的重复图形中突然插一个不同物，受试会高估它持续的时间。一种解释是“相对注意器资源”：新奇事物吸走了更多注意力与编码资源，让大脑事后回头估算时，错把它当作一个更长的过程。这个效应提醒我们：主观时间的长短，不来自一个客观的时钟，而是由大脑对当时处理强度的事后推断。
detailEn: Insert an oddball stimulus into a stream of identical shapes and people overestimate how long it lasted. The favoured account is that novel events claim extra attention and encoding, so a later reconstruction mistakes that density for a longer span. Subjective duration seems to be inferred from processing load, not read off a clock.

term: 工作会膨胀，填满你给它的所有时间
oneLiner: 截止越宽裕，任务越会被拖长、变复杂。
oneLinerEn: Give a task more time, and it expands to soak up every minute.
detail: 帕金森观察官僚体系发现：工作量的增加并不真正反映需要，而多受可用人数与时间驱动。延伸到个人：“为完成一件事预留一个月，它就会自然膨胀到填满一个月”。宽裕的截止日会鼓励提前推演、中途扩展、末尾重做。真正拉开效率的，往往不是“更努力”，而是“把可选时间人为地缩窄”。
detailEn: Parkinson noticed that bureaucratic work multiplies to fill available staff and time. The same holds for individuals: give a task a month, and it swells to consume the month. Loose deadlines invite early rehearsal, mid-course expansion, and last-minute rework. Tightening available time, not effort, often restores pace.

term: 未来的奖励，在当下会打折
oneLiner: 同样一块钱，拿得越早就越“大”；我们偏眼前的方式很系统。
oneLinerEn: A reward shrinks the further into the future it sits — and it shrinks in a predictable curve.
detail: “今天领100 还是一个月后领110？”很多人选前者。艾姆斯里发现，人对延迟的贴现不是指数曲线，而是“双曲线”：越接近当下，“再等一小会”的代价主观上越高。这解释了为何新年计划到周三就抛到九霄云外。大脑并非不会为未来打算，而是它的“折价器”在即时面前会剧烈短路。
detailEn: 'Take 100 today or 110 in a month?' Many choose the smaller-now. Ainslie showed that delay discounts hyperbolically rather than exponentially: the nearer a reward, the steeper its subjective drop-off for each extra day. New Year plans crumble by midweek not from weak logic but from a steeper discount curve close to the present.

term: 忙时飞，闲时慢：两种时间估计用两套系统
oneLiner: 实时估时和事后回忆估时，经常给出相反的答案。
oneLinerEn: Judging time as it flies and judging it after often gives opposite answers.
detail: 一段被事件填满的两小时，实时估时感觉“很长”，但往回看却“一掠而过”；一段什么都不发生的等待，实时难熬，回忆里却塌成很短一片。奥恩斯坦等人的工作显示，“预测式计时”与“回溯式计时”使用不同的机制。我们以为有一个统一的“时间感”，其实当下与回忆里的时间，是两个不同的系统在分别处理。
detailEn: A busy two hours feels long while it runs yet flashes by in memory; a waiting-room stretch feels endless live yet collapses on recall. Ornstein showed prospective and retrospective timing use different machinery. There is no single 'feel for time' — the live and the remembered clocks disagree by design.

term: 恐惧来临时，时间仿佛变慢
oneLiner: 怕的时候，主观秒变慢，虽然客观时钟照旧。
oneLinerEn: Under threat the felt second dilates even though the clock is unchanged.
detail: 德鲁瓦-沃莱等人的回顾发现，情绪唤起会拉长人对时长的估计，尤以恐惧为甚。威胁刺激吸走注意资源、并加速内部的“起搏器”，让一段定长的时间被归为“更长”。这也部分解释了事故幸存者常说的“那一瞬像慢镜头”：并非真的录到了更多帧，而是情绪让回忆时把内容读得更密。
detailEn: Droit-Volet and Gil reviewed evidence that arousal stretches felt duration, fear especially. Threatening stimuli pull attention and speed the internal pacemaker, tilting estimates of a fixed interval toward 'long'. Survivors' talk of 'seeing it in slow motion' may reflect memory read at higher density rather than literally more frames.

term: 拖延不是懒，而是为未来的自己透支
oneLiner: 我们总把任务“转给了未来的自己”，并默认他更扛得起。
oneLinerEn: We hand tasks to our future self and assume that stranger will cope.
detail: 神经影像发现，拖延者在想到“自己”时，激活模式更像想到一个陌生人，而非想到现在。于是“下周三开始”把代价都推给了“那个周三的自己”。时隔越远，那个未来越像别人，“他的负担”自然不太心疼。拖延不是不会规划，而是“未来自我”在你的共情地图上，本来就离得很远。
detailEn: Neuroimaging work suggests that for chronic procrastinators, thinking of 'the future me' lights patterns closer to thinking of a stranger than of the present self. So 'I'll start next Wednesday' dumps the burden on that near-foreign figure. Procrastination is not a planning failure but a self-continuity gap across time.

term: 我们用空间来「想」时间
oneLiner: “前”“后”“近”“远”……你对时间的概念，其实是借自身体朝向。
oneLinerEn: Words like 'ahead', 'behind', 'near' leak the spatial scaffolding underneath time.
detail: 我们说“下周前”“把过去落在后头”，但时间本无前后。博罗季茨基实验发现，当身体姿势被隐式调整（比如朝某方向轻微倾斜），受试判断时间语句的速度会变；而汉语使用者有时垂直地组织时间（上个月“上”、下个月“下”）。抽象的时间概念背后，装着一个由身体与语言提供的坐标系。
detailEn: We speak of 'the week ahead' and 'leaving the past behind', yet time has no front. Boroditsky's experiments showed that subtly tilting the body bends the speed of temporal judgements, and Mandarin speakers often run time vertically (shàng ge yuè 'last month' is literally up-month). Abstract time reasoning inherits a coordinate frame built by body plus language.

term: “准备电位”可能只是噪声跨过了阈值
oneLiner: 利贝特的著名结果，可能高估了无意识启动的分量。
oneLinerEn: Libet's famous lead may be an artefact of noisy brain signals crossing a threshold.
detail: 谢格尔等人重新分析发现：所谓“决定前就升起的准备电位”，可能只是大脑背景噪声的随机涨落，当它向上跨过某个阈值时动作就发生。把这些信号反向从行时，“意识决定晚于启动”的时间差就大为缩水。这不等于推翻利贝特，却提醒我们：同一个脑电现象，可以讲出完全相反的故事。关于自由意志的著名实验，远未盖棺。
detailEn: Schurger and colleagues showed that the readiness potential may be random neural noise that crosses a threshold to trigger a move; when signals are back-projected, the 'decision comes too late' gap shrinks. This does not refute Libet but warns that one brain signal can support opposite stories. The famous free-will experiment remains unsettled.

term: 一旦不信自由意志，人更容易作弊
oneLiner: 仅仅是读到“人没有自由意志”，随后作弊、虚报的比率就会上升。
oneLinerEn: Reading that free will is an illusion makes cheating and stealing a little likelier.
detail: 沃斯与斯科勒让受试阅读否定自由意志的文章，随后让他们在一个容易虚报成绩的任务上表现。结果：被启动“不信自由意志”的一组作弊更多，且事后并不觉得更差。因为当人们不再相信“我能选、要负责”时，“责任”这个概念也跟着被卸下了。有趣的是，这一效应与是否“真的”有自由意志无关——它关乎信什么会如何改变行为。
detailEn: Vohs and Schooler had people read passages denying free will, then offered an easy chance to cheat. Those primed to disbelieve cheated more, without feeling worse. When 'I could have chosen otherwise' fades, responsibility thins with it. The effect is about what believing does to conduct, not whether free will is metaphysically real.

term: 错觉控制：明明无关，却觉得“我能影响它”
oneLiner: 越是亲手参与，就越容易把巧合看成因果，相信自己能影响随机。
oneLinerEn: Personal involvement makes chance feel influenceable, biasing bets and choices.
detail: 兰杰让受试按自己选的号码或随机分配的号码抽签，发现人们对自己选的那张估值更高、也更愿换。在本质上全机率的事件里，只要中间夹着一个“我的选择”，人们就把它当成“我多一分控制”的证据。从掷骰子到股市下注，这种错觉把随机重读为技艺。它有时是动力，但有时让人付出真金白银。
detailEn: Langer found that people value a lottery ticket they picked over one handed to them, even though the odds are identical. Insert 'I chose' into a purely chance event and it reads as 'I have some control'. Dice, stocks and prayers all fall to this. The illusion can fuel effort, yet it also drains wallets.

term: 左脑解释器：为“我的决定”现编理由
oneLiner: 当一半大脑各行其是，“我”的解释却能无缝自圆。
oneLinerEn: Split brains act on one impulse yet the 'I' offers a smooth reason for another.
detail: 加扎尼加研究裂脑人：右脑收到“走开”的指令后起身离开，当被问及为何这么做，信使般的左脑半球不假思索地编出一个看似合理的理由（“我想去拿罐汽水”），而它自己并不知道真正原因。这个“解释器”会不断为我们无意识发起的行为配一个连贯的“我为什么这么做”。你以为的“我自主决定”，有时是事后生成的叙事。
detailEn: Gazzaniga's split-brain patients acted on a command given to one hemisphere, and the other — asked to explain — confidently invented a reason it could not know. This 'interpreter' keeps weaving coherent 'why I did it' stories around behaviour started elsewhere. The sense of authorship may be narration generated after the fact.

term: 大脑把“意图”和“动作”往一起挤
oneLiner: 当你觉得“是我按的键”，主观上意图与动作的间隔会缩短。
oneLinerEn: When you feel you caused a press, the intent and action fuse closer in reported time.
detail: 哈格德等人让受试自己按一个键（意图与动作相隔约十分之一秒），回报时间时会把它们“挤得更近”；而当键由外界触发时，这种压缩消失。也就是说，我们不但对“我做了”有临场感，对“何时决定”的记忆也会因“我是发起者”而变形。主观上的“我决定—我动手”那段距离，其实是一个被因果感捏过的橡皮时间。
detailEn: Haggard showed that when you freely press a key, the reported times of intent and action pull closer together; when the press is externally triggered, the shrinkage vanishes. Sense of agency not only marks 'I did it' but rewrites when you think you decided. The felt gap between 'decide' and 'do' is rubber bent by causality.

term: 说不清的偏好，我们都能编个理由
oneLiner: 我们很难看穿自己真正为何选择，却总能流畅地给出“原因”。
oneLinerEn: We cannot see why we chose, yet can always rattle off a reason.
detail: 尼斯伯特与威尔逊的经典回顾指出：人对“自己为何这样选”的报告，很多时候并不反映真正起作用的因素。当某个无关变量（位置、先入为主的提示）改变了选择，人们不会提到它，而是编一个听起来合理的原因。这不是因为人在撒谎，而是内省本身就拿不到那些驱动决定的过程。我们既高估了“知道自己为何”，也据此高估了“自己能选”。
detailEn: Nisbett and Wilson's classic review held that people's reports of why they chose often miss the factors actually at work. When an irrelevant variable (position, a prior prime) shifts the pick, people never mention it; they confabulate a plausible reason instead. Not lying but limited access: introspection cannot reach the processes that drove the choice.

term: 催眠下，动作像是“从别处来的”
oneLiner: 同一个动作，当它是“自己动的”而非“被安排的”，主观感受完全不同。
oneLinerEn: The same movement feels unowned when it arrives via suggestion rather than decision.
detail: 阿米里安等人用“催眠挑战”发现：受试把手抬起，却报告“几乎没有主动感”，像是它自己动了。有趣的是，当同一动作是被暗示启动时，“我决定”的主观临场感会下降。这支持了一种观点：“意志感”不是动作本身的属性，而是大脑对动作来源的一项额外标签。当标签被改写，“我发起了它”也会变得不确定。
detailEn: Amiran and colleagues had participants lift a hand under hypnosis while reporting almost no sense of authorship: it felt as if the hand moved itself. Suggested actions lose the 'I initiated it' feel. The result supports treating sense of agency as a label added by the brain, not a property of the movement itself.

term: 自由意志也许是“刹车”，不是“引擎”
oneLiner: 也许我们无法启动动作，却能在最后一刻否决它。
oneLinerEn: We may not start an action, but we can still veto it at the last moment.
detail: 里贝特本人并不认为实验推翻了自由意志：他提出“自由否决权”——即使动作的早期酝酿是无意识的，意识仍能在最后阶段“踩住它”。谢尔的研究进一步发现，前脑存在与“停止”相关的独立信号。这一观点把自由意志从“我要做”，改写成“我可以不做”：决定不是唯一起点，拦阻也是。
detailEn: Libet himself held that consciousness might retain a 'veto' — a last-moment stop even if the action's build-up began unconsciously. Schall found dedicated 'stop' signals in prefrontal circuits. Reframed this way, free will may live less in initiation than in cancellation: not the engine we start but the brake we press.

term: “我动了”的感觉，来自大脑预测了后果
oneLiner: 当感觉与预期对得上，我们才觉得自己发起了动作。
oneLinerEn: We feel in charge when predicted and actual sensory outcomes line up.
detail: 沃尔珀特等人的“比较器”模型提出：大脑为动作发出一份“预测副本”，再拿它与实际感觉反馈对比。两者对得上，我们就标记为“是我干的”；若对不上（比如机器延迟了反馈），“我控制它”的主观感就会下降。一个直接推论是：“发起者感”不是一条硬事实，而是大脑基于预测匹配的一项推断。它也能解释部分幻听与“声音被外力控制”的体验。
detailEn: Wolpert's comparator model proposes that the brain files a predicted copy of each motor command and compares it with sensory feedback. When prediction and reality match, we tag the action as self-made; when a machine shifts the feedback, the felt sense of controlling it drops. Agency is inferred from prediction, not delivered as raw fact — a view that also sheds light on auditory hallucinations.

term: 四岁前，你其实不信「别人脑中和你不同」
oneLiner: 4 岁前，孩子默认「只要我知道，别人也一定知道」。
oneLinerEn: Before about four, children assume what you know, everyone knows.
detail: 萨莉-安任务：萨莉把球放篮子里离开，安把球挪到盒子里；问孩子“萨莉回来会去哪找”——4 岁前几乎全答“盒子”，因为他无法建立“萨莉不知道”的内部模型。Wellman 等人的元分析发现，这个“读心里程碑”在不同语言与文化中都在 4–5 岁出现；自闭症儿童在这条路上明显更晚。你以为“读心”是天生本能，其实它是一个需要几年才点亮的推断模型。
detailEn: In the Sally-Anne task, children under four say Sally will look where the ball actually is, not where she believes it to be. Wellman's meta-analysis shows this 'theory-of-mind' milestone lands around four to five across cultures; autistic children reach it later or not at all. Reading minds feels innate but is a model that must come online.

term: 会爬的婴儿，能「看见」看不见的深渊
oneLiner: 刚会爬的婴儿在玻璃「悬崖」前止步——深度知觉早于危险感。
oneLinerEn: New crawlers refuse the glass 'cliff'—depth perception arrives before any lesson in danger.
detail: Gibson 与 Walk 让婴儿坐在“视觉悬崖”一边，另一边看似落差巨大，实则盖着厚玻璃。多数刚会爬的婴儿拒绝越过；即使被鼓动，他们会犹豫、探探、退回。深度知觉在语言与“小心”教育之前就已就位，动作经验才是把它变成行为的钥匙。所谓“怕高”并非天生，而是会爬之后才被重新激活的。
detailEn: Gibson and Walk placed infants on one side of a 'cliff' covered by safety glass. Most refused to crawl over despite coaxing; they hesitated, patted the surface, then retreated. Depth perception is online long before any lesson about danger. Fear of heights is not innate but recruited once the baby can move on its own.

term: 孩子会「照抄」大人那些明显没用的动作
oneLiner: 明明只需一步就能打开盒子，孩子仍会坚持照做十步「仪式」。
oneLinerEn: Children faithfully replay every useless step of a demonstration they could shortcut.
detail: 成人会省略无关步骤，孩子却一丝不苟地模仿全部——包括显然多余的。Lyons 等人发现，2–3 岁的幼儿在面对“只有一步管用”的装置时，仍会忠实把演示者的仪式一并照做。这可能恰恰是人类学习超级能力的一面：在不知道因果的时候，宁可“全盘照抄”也不误丢关键。孩子不是不懂变通，他们在用最保守的方式，把大人的世界整个搬进自己脑子里。
detailEn: Where adults skip useless steps, children replay them all. Lyons et al. found that two-year-olds faithfully copied demonstrator 'rituals' on a box whose solution was obviously one move. This over-copying is a learning strategy: when you do not yet know what matters, copy everything rather than prune by mistake.

term: 小孩判断对错，看后果不看意图
oneLiner: 打碎 15 个杯子的“好心”孩子，被 5 岁小孩判得比打碎 1 个的“坏心”更重。
oneLinerEn: To a five-year-old, the boy who broke fifteen cups 'by accident' is worse than the one who broke one while sneaking jam.
detail: 皮亚杰的经典对偶故事：一个孩子不小心撞碎一打杯子，另一个偷果酱时打碎一只。5 岁上下的孩子判前者更坏，理由直白——“他打碎的更多”。到 8–10 岁，“故意 vs 意外”的意图维度才逐渐上位。这不是孩子“坏”，而是他们的道德操作系统先建“结果账本”，再补“意图模块”。你以为的“天生明辨是非”，其实是一个需要十年才能装齐的软件。
detailEn: Piaget's paired stories pitted an 'accident' that broke a dozen cups against a 'naughty' act that broke one.
